entries.86dfafb6bb81b036f23d2d0126a26a309c20662f: <div sID="gen21433" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="Matt.5" sID="Matt.5"/> <div eID="gen21433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21434" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21435" type="x-p"/> This chapter, and the two that follow it, are a sermon; a famous sermon; the sermon upon the mount. It is the longest and fullest continued discourse of our Saviour that we have upon record in all the gospels. It is a practical discourse; there is not much of the credenda of Christianity in it—the things to be believed, but it is wholly taken up with the agenda—the things to be done; these Christ began with in his preaching; for if any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God. The circumstances of the sermon being accounted for (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.1-Matt.5.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>), the sermon itself follows, the scope of which is, not to fill our heads with notions, but to guide and regulate our practice. I. He proposes blessedness as the end, and gives us the character of those who are entitled to blessedness (very different from the sentiments of a vain world), in eight beatitudes, which may justly be called paradoxes, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.3-Matt.5.12">ver. 3-12</reference>. II. He prescribes duty as the way, and gives us standing rules of that duty. He directs his disciples, 1. To understand what they are—the salt of the earth, and the lights of the world, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.13-Matt.5.16">ver. 13-16</reference>. 2. To understand what they have to do—they are to be governed by the moral law. Here is, (1.) A general ratification of the law, and a recommendation of it to us, as our rule, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.17-Matt.5.20">ver. 17-20</reference>. (2.) A particular rectification of divers mistakes; or, rather, a reformation of divers wilful, gross corruptions, which the scribes and Pharisees had introduced in their exposition of the law; and an authentic explication of divers branches which most needed to be explained and vindicated, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.20">ver. 20</reference>. Particularly, here is an explication, [1.] Of the sixth commandment, which forbids murder, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.21-Matt.5.26">ver. 21-26</reference>. [2.] Of the seventh commandment, against adultery, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.27-Matt.5.32">ver. 27-32</reference>. [3.] Of the third commandment, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.33-Matt.5.37">ver. 33-37</reference>. [4.] Of the law of retaliation, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.38-Matt.5.42">ver. 38-42</reference>. [5.] Of the law of brotherly love, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.43-Matt.5.48">ver. 43-48</reference>. And the scope of the whole is, to show that the law is spiritual.
entries.db8e982c21e55689f46105d429aa33168dc57b07: <div eID="gen21435" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21434" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sermon on the Mount.</title> <div sID="gen21436" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And seeing the multitudes, he went up into a mountain: and when he was set, his disciples came unto him: <hi type="super">2</hi> And he opened his mouth, and taught them, saying, <div eID="gen21436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21437" type="x-p"/> We have here a general account of this sermon. <div eID="gen21437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21438" type="x-p"/> I. <hi type="italic">The Preacher</hi> was our Lord Jesus, the Prince of preachers, the great Prophet of his church, who <hi type="italic">came into the world,</hi> to be <hi type="italic">the Light of the world.</hi> The prophets and John had <hi type="italic">done virtuously</hi> in preaching, <hi type="italic">but</hi> Christ <hi type="italic">excelled them all.</hi> He is the eternal Wisdom, <hi type="italic">that lay in the bosom of the Father, before all worlds,</hi> and perfectly knew his will (<reference osisRef="John.1.18">John i. 18</reference>); and he is the eternal Word, by whom he <hi type="italic">has in these last days spoken to us.</hi> The many miraculous cures wrought by Christ in Galilee, which we read of in the close of the foregoing chapter, were intended to make way for this sermon, and to dispose people to receive instructions from one in whom there appeared so much of a divine power and goodness; and, probably, this sermon was the summary, or rehearsal, of what he had preached up and down in the synagogues of Galilee. His text <hi type="italic">was, Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.</hi> This is a sermon on the former part of that text, showing what it is to <hi type="italic">repent;</hi> it is to reform, both in judgment and practice; and here he tells us wherein, in answer to that question (<reference osisRef="Mal.3.7">Mal. iii. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">Wherein shall we return?</hi> He afterward preached upon the latter part of the text, when, in divers parables, he showed what the kingdom of heaven is like, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.1-Matt.13.52">ch. xiii.</reference> <div eID="gen21438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21439" type="x-p"/> II. <hi type="italic">The place</hi> was a mountain in Galilee. As in other things, so in this, our Lord Jesus was but ill accommodated; he had no convenient place to preach in, any more than <hi type="italic">to lay his head</hi> on. While the scribes and Pharisees had Moses' chair to sit in, with all possible ease, honour, and state, and there corrupted the law; our Lord Jesus, the great Teacher of truth, is driven out to the desert, and finds no better a pulpit than <hi type="italic">a mountain</hi> can afford; and not one of the <hi type="italic">holy mountains</hi> neither, not one of <hi type="italic">the mountains of Zion,</hi> but a common <hi type="italic">mountain;</hi> by which Christ would intimate that there is no such distinguishing holiness of places now, under the gospel, as there was under the law; but that it is <hi type="italic">the will of God that men should pray</hi> and preach <hi type="italic">every where,</hi> any where, provided it be decent and convenient. Christ preached this sermon, which was an exposition of the law, upon a mountain, because upon a <hi type="italic">mountain</hi> the law was given; and this was also a solemn promulgation of the Christian law. But observe the difference: when <hi type="italic">the law was given,</hi> the Lord <hi type="italic">came down</hi> upon the <hi type="italic">mountain;</hi> now the Lord <hi type="italic">went up:</hi> then, he spoke <hi type="italic">in thunder and lightning;</hi> now, <hi type="italic">in a still small voice:</hi> then the people were ordered to keep their distance; now they are invited to draw near: a blessed change! If God's grace and goodness are (as they certainly are) his glory, then the glory of the gospel is the glory that excels, for <hi type="italic">grace and truth came by Jesus Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.7">2 Cor. iii. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.18">Heb. xii. 18</reference>, &c. It was foretold of Zebulun and Issachar, two of the tribes of Galilee (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.19">Deut. xxxiii. 19</reference>), that <hi type="italic">they shall call the people to the mountain;</hi> to this <hi type="italic">mountain</hi> we are called, to learn <hi type="italic">to offer the sacrifices of righteousness.</hi> Now was this <hi type="italic">the mountain of the Lord,</hi> where he <hi type="italic">taught us his ways,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.2.2-Isa.2.3">Isa. ii. 2, 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.4.1-Mic.4.2">Mic. iv. 1, 2</reference>. <div eID="gen21439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21440" type="x-p"/> III. <hi type="italic">The auditors</hi> were <hi type="italic">his disciples,</hi> who <hi type="italic">came unto him;</hi> came at his call, as appears by comparing <reference osisRef="Mark.3.13">Mark iii. 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.6.13">Luke vi. 13</reference>. To them he directed his speech, because they followed him for love and learning, while others attended him only for cures. <hi type="italic">He taught them,</hi> because they were willing to be <hi type="italic">taught (the meek will he teach his way</hi>); because they would <hi type="italic">understand</hi> what he taught, which to others was foolishness; and because they were to teach others; and it was therefore requisite that they should have a clear and distinct knowledge of these things themselves. The duties prescribed in this sermon were to be conscientiously performed by all those that would <hi type="italic">enter into that kingdom of heaven</hi> which they were sent to set up, with hope to have the benefit of it. But though this discourse was directed to the disciples, it was in the hearing of <hi type="italic">the multitude;</hi> for it is said (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.28">ch. vii. 28</reference>), <hi type="italic">The people were astonished.</hi> No bounds were set about <hi type="italic">this mountain,</hi> to keep the people off, as were about <hi type="italic">mount Sinai</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.12">Exod. xix. 12</reference>); for, through Christ, we have access to God, not only to speak to him, but to hear from him. Nay, he had an eye to the <hi type="italic">multitude,</hi> in preaching this sermon. When the fame of his miracles had brought a vast crowd together, he took the opportunity of so great a confluence of people, to instruct them. Note, It is an encouragement to a faithful minister to cast the net of the gospel where there are a great many fishes, in hope that some will be caught. The sight of a <hi type="italic">multitude</hi> puts life into a preacher, which yet must arise from a desire of their profit, not his own praise. <div eID="gen21440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21441" type="x-p"/> IV. <hi type="italic">The solemnity</hi> of his sermon is intimated in that word, <hi type="italic">when he was set.</hi> Christ preached many times occasionally, and by interlocutory discourses; but this was a set sermon, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">kathisantos autou</hi></hi>, when he had placed himself so as to be best heard. He sat down as a Judge or Lawgiver. It intimates with what sedateness and composure of mind the things of God should be spoken and heard. <hi type="italic">He sat,</hi> that <hi type="italic">the scriptures might be fulfilled</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mal.3.3">Mal. iii. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">He shall sit as a refiner,</hi> to purge away the dross, the corrupt doctrines of the sons of Levi. He <hi type="italic">sat</hi> as <hi type="italic">in the throne, judging right</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.4">Ps. ix. 4</reference>); for <hi type="italic">the word he spoke shall judge us.</hi> That phrase, <hi type="italic">He opened his mouth,</hi> is only a Hebrew periphrasis of speaking, as <reference osisRef="Job.3.1">Job iii. 1</reference>. Yet some think it intimates the solemnity of this discourse; the congregation being large, he raised his voice, and spoke louder than usual. He had spoken long <hi type="italic">by his servants the prophets,</hi> and <hi type="italic">opened their mouths</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.3.27">Ezek. iii. 27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.27">xxiv. 27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.22">xxxiii. 22</reference>); but now <hi type="italic">he opened his</hi> own, and spoke with freedom, <hi type="italic">as one having authority.</hi> One of the ancients has this remark upon it; Christ <hi type="italic">taught</hi> much without <hi type="italic">opening his mouth.</hi> that is, by his holy and exemplary life; nay, he <hi type="italic">taught,</hi> when, being <hi type="italic">led as a lamb to the slaughter, he opened not his mouth,</hi> but now <hi type="italic">he opened his mouth, and taught,</hi> that <hi type="italic">the scriptures might be fulfilled,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.8.1-Prov.8.2">Prov. viii. 1, 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.6">6</reference>. <hi type="italic">Doth not wisdom cry—cry on the top of high places?</hi> And <hi type="italic">the opening of her lips shall be right things. He taught them,</hi> according to the promise (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.13">Isa. liv. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">All thy children shall be taught of the Lord;</hi> for this purpose he had <hi type="italic">the tongue of the learned</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.4">Isa. l. 4</reference>), and <hi type="italic">the Spirit of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">Isa. lxi. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">He taught them,</hi> what was the evil they should abhor, and what was the good they should abide and abound in; for Christianity is not a matter of speculation, but is designed to regulate the temper of our minds and the tenour of our conversations; gospel-time is a time of reformation (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.10">Heb. ix. 10</reference>); and by the gospel we must be reformed, must be made good, must be made better. <hi type="italic">The truth, as it is in Jesus,</hi> is <hi type="italic">the truth which is according to godliness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.1.1">Tit. i. 1</reference>.
entries.65728732de2c9796cbe029d16afd17ef21349c2a: <div eID="gen21441" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sermon on the Mount.</title> <div sID="gen21442" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">are</hi> the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. <hi type="super">4</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">are</hi> they that mourn: for they shall be comforted. <hi type="super">5</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">are</hi> the meek: for they shall inherit the earth. <hi type="super">6</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">are</hi> they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled. <hi type="super">7</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">are</hi> the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy. <hi type="super">8</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">are</hi> the pure in heart: for they shall see God. 9 Blessed <hi type="italic">are</hi> the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God. <hi type="super">10</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">are</hi> they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. <hi type="super">11</hi> Blessed are ye, when <hi type="italic">men</hi> shall revile you, and persecute <hi type="italic">you,</hi> and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake. <hi type="super">12</hi> Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great <hi type="italic">is</hi> your reward in heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you. <div eID="gen21442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21443" type="x-p"/> Christ begins his sermon with blessings, for <hi type="italic">he came into the world to bless us</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.3.26">Acts iii. 26</reference>), as <hi type="italic">the great High Priest of our profession;</hi> as <hi type="italic">the blessed Melchizedec;</hi> as He <hi type="italic">in whom all the families of the earth should be blessed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.12.3">Gen. xii. 3</reference>. He came not only to purchase blessings for us, but to pour out and pronounce blessings on us; and here he does it <hi type="italic">as one having authority,</hi> as one that can <hi type="italic">command the blessing, even life for evermore,</hi> and that is the blessing here again and again promised to the good; his pronouncing them happy makes them so; for those whom he blesses, are blessed indeed. The Old Testament ended with a curse (<reference osisRef="Mal.4.6">Mal. iv. 6</reference>), the gospel begins with a blessing; for <hi type="italic">hereunto are we called, that we should inherit the blessing.</hi> Each of the blessings Christ here pronounces has a double intention: 1. To show who they are that are to be accounted truly happy, and what their characters are. 2. What that is wherein true happiness consists, in the promises made to persons of certain characters, the performance of which will make them happy. Now, <div eID="gen21443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21444" type="x-p"/> 1. This is designed to rectify the ruinous mistakes of a blind and carnal world. Blessedness is the thing which men pretend to pursue; <hi type="italic">Who will make us to see good?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.4.6">Ps. iv. 6</reference>. But most mistake the end, and form a wrong notion of happiness; and then no wonder that they miss the way; they choose their own delusions, and court a shadow. The general opinion is, <hi type="italic">Blessed are they</hi> that are rich, and great, and honourable in the world; they spend their days in mirth, and their years in pleasure; they eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and carry all before them with a high hand, and have every sheaf bowing to their sheaf; <hi type="italic">happy the people that is in such a case;</hi> and their designs, aims, and purposes are accordingly; they <hi type="italic">bless the covetous</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.3">Ps. x. 3</reference>); they <hi type="italic">will be rich.</hi> Now our Lord Jesus comes to correct this fundamental error, to advance a new hypothesis, and to give us quite another notion of blessedness and blessed people, which, however paradoxical it may appear to those who are prejudiced, yet is in itself, and appears to be to all who are savingly enlightened, a rule and doctrine of eternal truth and certainty, by which we must shortly be judged. If this, therefore, be the beginning of Christ's doctrine, the beginning of a Christian's practice must be to take his measures of happiness from those maxims, and to direct his pursuits accordingly. <div eID="gen21444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21445" type="x-p"/> 2. It is designed to remove the discouragements of the weak and poor who receive the gospel, by assuring them that his gospel did not make those only happy that were eminent in gifts, graces, comforts, and usefulness; but that even <hi type="italic">the least in the kingdom of heaven,</hi> whose heart was upright with God, was happy in the honours and privileges of that kingdom. <div eID="gen21445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21446" type="x-p"/> 3. It is designed to invite souls to Christ, and to make way for his law into their hearts. Christ's pronouncing these blessings, not at the end of his sermon, to dismiss the people, but at the beginning of it, to prepare them for what he had further to say to them, may remind us of mount Gerizim and mount Ebal, on which the blessings and cursings of the law were read, <reference osisRef="Deut.27.12">Deut. xxvii. 12</reference>, &c. <hi type="italic">There</hi> the curses are expressed, and the blessings only implied; <hi type="italic">here</hi> the blessings are expressed, and the curses implied: in both, <hi type="italic">life and death are set before us;</hi> but the law appeared more as a ministration of death, to deter us from sin; the gospel as a dispensation of life, to allure us to Christ, in whom alone all good is to be had. And those who had seen the gracious cures wrought by his hand (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.23-Matt.4.24">ch. iv. 23, 24</reference>), and now heard <hi type="italic">the gracious words proceeding out of his mouth,</hi> would say that he was all of a piece, made up of love and sweetness. <div eID="gen21446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21447" type="x-p"/> 4. It is designed to settle and sum up the articles of agreement between God and man. The scope of the divine revelation is to let us know what God expects from us, and what we may then expect from him; and no where is this more fully set forth in a few words than here, nor with a more exact reference to each other; and this is that gospel which we are required to believe; for what is faith but a conformity to these characters, and a dependence upon these promises? The way to happiness is here opened, and made a <hi type="italic">highway</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.35.8">Isa. xxxv. 8</reference>); and this coming from the mouth of Jesus Christ, it is intimated that from him, and by him, we are to receive both the seed and the fruit, both the grace required, and the glory promised. Nothing passes between God and fallen man, but through his hand. Some of the wiser heathen had notions of blessedness different from the rest of mankind, and looking toward this of our Saviour. Seneca, undertaking to describe a blessed man, makes it out, that it is only an honest, good man that is to be so called: <hi type="italic">De vita beata.</hi> cap. 4. <hi type="italic">Cui nullum bonum malumque sit, nisi bonus malusque animus—Quem nec extollant fortuita, nec frangant—Cui vera voluptas erit voluptatum comtemplio—Cui unum bonum honestas, unum malum turpitudo.—In whose estimation nothing is good or evil, but a good or evil heart—Whom no occurrences elate or deject—Whose true pleasure consists in a contempt of pleasure—To whom the only good is virtue, and the only evil vice.</hi> <div eID="gen21447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21448" type="x-p"/> Our Saviour here gives us eight characters of blessed people; which represent to us the principal graces of a Christian. On each of them a present blessing is pronounced; <hi type="italic">Blessed are</hi> they; and to each a future blessing is promised, which is variously expressed, so as to suit the nature of the grace or duty recommended. <div eID="gen21448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21449" type="x-p"/> Do we ask then who are happy? It is answered, <div eID="gen21449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21450" type="x-p"/> I. <hi type="italic">The poor in spirit</hi> are happy, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.3">v. 3</reference>. There is a poor-spiritedness that is so far from making men blessed that it is a sin and a snare—cowardice and base fear, and a willing subjection to the lusts of men. But this poverty of spirit is a gracious disposition of soul, by which we are emptied of self, in order to our being filled with Jesus Christ. To be <hi type="italic">poor in spirit</hi> is, 1. To be contentedly poor, willing to be emptied of worldly wealth, if God orders that to be our lot; to bring our mind to our condition, when it is a low condition. Many are poor in the world, but high in spirit, poor and proud, murmuring and complaining, and blaming their lot, but we must accommodate ourselves to our poverty, must <hi type="italic">know how to be abased,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.4.12">Phil. iv. 12</reference>. Acknowledging the wisdom of God in appointing us to poverty, we must be easy in it, patiently bear the inconveniences of it, be thankful for what we have, and make the best of that which is. It is to sit loose to all worldly wealth, and not set our hearts upon it, but cheerfully to bear losses and disappointments which may befal us in the most prosperous state. It is not, in pride or pretence, to make ourselves poor, by throwing away what God has given us, especially as those in the church of Rome, who vow poverty, and yet engross the wealth of the nations; but if we be rich in the world we must be <hi type="italic">poor in spirit,</hi> that is, we must condescend to the poor and sympathize with them, as being touched with the feeling of their infirmities; we must expect and prepare for poverty; must not inordinately fear or shun it, but must bid it welcome, especially when it comes upon us for keeping a good conscience, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.34">Heb. x. 34</reference>. Job was <hi type="italic">poor in spirit,</hi> when he blessed God in <hi type="italic">taking away,</hi> as well as giving. 2. It is to be humble and lowly in our own eyes. To be <hi type="italic">poor in spirit,</hi> is to think meanly of ourselves, of what we are, and have, and do; the poor are often taken in the Old Testament for the humble and self-denying, as opposed to those that are at ease, and the proud; it is to be as little children in our opinion of ourselves, weak, foolish, and insignificant, <reference osisRef="Matt.18.4">ch. xviii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.19.14">xix. 14</reference>. Laodicea was <hi type="italic">poor in spirituals,</hi> wretchedly and miserably poor, and yet <hi type="italic">rich in spirit,</hi> so well increased with goods, as to <hi type="italic">have need of nothing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.17">Rev. iii. 17</reference>. On the other hand, Paul was rich in <hi type="italic">spirituals,</hi> excelling most in gifts and graces, and yet <hi type="italic">poor in spirit, the least of the apostles,</hi> less than the least of all saints, and <hi type="italic">nothing</hi> in his own account. It is to look with a holy contempt upon ourselves, to value others and undervalue ourselves in comparison of them. It is to be willing to make ourselves cheap, and mean, and little, to do good; to <hi type="italic">become all things to all men.</hi> It is to acknowledge that God is great, and we are mean; that he is holy and we are sinful; that he is all and we are nothing, less than nothing, worse than nothing; and to humble ourselves before him, and under his mighty hand. 3. It is to come off from all confidence in our own righteousness and strength, that we may depend only upon the merit of Christ for our justification, and the spirit and grace of Christ for our sanctification. That <hi type="italic">broken and contrite spirit</hi> with which the publican cried for mercy to a poor sinner, is that poverty of spirit. We must call ourselves poor, because always in want of God's grace, always begging at God's door, always hanging on in his house. <div eID="gen21450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21451" type="x-p"/> Now, (1.) This poverty in spirit is put first among the Christian graces. The philosophers did not reckon humility among their moral virtues, but Christ puts it first. Self-denial is the first lesson to be learned in his school, and poverty of spirit entitled to the first beatitude. The foundation of all other graces is laid in humility. Those who would build high must begin low; and it is an excellent preparative for the entrance of gospel-grace into the soul; it fits the soil to receive the seed. Those <hi type="italic">who are weary and heavy laden,</hi> are <hi type="italic">the poor in spirit,</hi> and they shall find rest with Christ. <div eID="gen21451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21452" type="x-p"/> (2.) They are <hi type="italic">blessed.</hi> Now they are so, in this world. God looks graciously upon them. They are his little ones, and have their angels. To them he gives more grace; they live the most comfortable lives, and are easy to themselves and all about them, and nothing comes amiss to them; while high spirits are always uneasy. <div eID="gen21452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21453" type="x-p"/> (3.) <hi type="italic">Theirs is the kingdom of heaven.</hi> The kingdom of <hi type="italic">grace</hi> is composed of such; they only are fit to be members of Christ's church, which is called <hi type="italic">the congregation of the poor</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.19">Ps. lxxiv. 19</reference>); the kingdom of <hi type="italic">glory</hi> is prepared for them. Those who thus humble themselves, and comply with God when he humbles them, shall be thus exalted. The great, high spirits go away with the glory of <hi type="italic">the kingdoms of the earth;</hi> but the humble, mild, and yielding souls obtain the glory of <hi type="italic">the kingdom of heaven.</hi> We are ready to think concerning those who are rich, and do good with their riches, that, no doubt, <hi type="italic">theirs is the kingdom of heaven;</hi> for they can thus lay up in store a good security <hi type="italic">for the time to come;</hi> but what shall the poor do, who have not wherewithal to do good? Why, the same happiness is promised to those who are contentedly poor, as to those who are usefully rich. If I am not able to <hi type="italic">spend</hi> cheerfully for his sake, if I can but <hi type="italic">want</hi> cheerfully for his sake, even that shall be recompensed. And do not we serve a good master then? <div eID="gen21453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21454" type="x-p"/> II. <hi type="italic">They that mourn</hi> are happy (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.4">v. 4</reference>); <hi type="italic">Blessed are they that mourn.</hi> This is another strange blessing, and fitly follows the former. The poor are accustomed to mourn, the graciously poor mourn graciously. We are apt to think, Blessed are the <hi type="italic">merry;</hi> but Christ, who was himself a great mourner, says, Blessed are the <hi type="italic">mourners.</hi> There is a sinful mourning, which is an enemy to blessedness—<hi type="italic">the sorrow of the world;</hi> despairing melancholy upon a spiritual account, and disconsolate grief upon a temporal account. There is a natural mourning, which may prove a friend to blessedness, by the grace of God working with it, and sanctifying the afflictions to us, for which we mourn. But there is a gracious mourning, which qualifies for blessedness, an habitual seriousness, the mind mortified to mirth, and an actual sorrow. 1. A penitential mourning for our own sins; this is <hi type="italic">godly sorrow,</hi> a sorrow according to God; sorrow for sin, with an eye to Christ, <reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">Zech. xii. 10</reference>. Those are God's mourners, who live a life of repentance, who lament the corruption of their nature, and their many actual transgressions, and God's withdrawings from them; and who, out of regard to God's honour, mourn also for the sins of others, and <hi type="italic">sigh and cry for their abominations,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.4">Ezek. ix. 4</reference>. 2. A sympathizing mourning for the afflictions of others; the mourning of those who <hi type="italic">weep with them that weep,</hi> are sorrowful <hi type="italic">for the solemn assemblies, for the desolations of Zion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zeph.3.18">Zeph. iii. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.137.1">Ps. cxxxvii. 1</reference>), especially who look with compassion on perishing souls, and <hi type="italic">weep over</hi> them, as Christ <hi type="italic">over Jerusalem.</hi> <div eID="gen21454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21455" type="x-p"/> Now these gracious mourners, (1.) <hi type="italic">Are blessed.</hi> As in vain and sinful <hi type="italic">laughter the heart is sorrowful,</hi> so in gracious mourning <hi type="italic">the heart</hi> has a serious joy, a secret satisfaction, which a <hi type="italic">stranger does not intermeddle with.</hi> They are <hi type="italic">blessed,</hi> for they are like the Lord Jesus, who <hi type="italic">was a man of sorrows,</hi> and of whom we never read that he laughed, but often that he wept. The are armed against the many temptations that attend vain mirth, and are prepared for the comforts of a sealed pardon and a settled peace. (2.) <hi type="italic">They shall be comforted.</hi> Though perhaps they are not immediately comforted, yet plentiful provision is made for their comfort; light is sown for them; and in heaven, it is certain, <hi type="italic">they shall be comforted,</hi> as Lazarus, <reference osisRef="Luke.16.25">Luke xvi. 25</reference>. Note, The happiness of heaven consists in being perfectly and eternally comforted, and in the <hi type="italic">wiping away of all tears from their eyes.</hi> It <hi type="italic">is the joy of our Lord; a fulness of joy and pleasures for evermore;</hi> which will be doubly sweet to those who have been prepared for them by this <hi type="italic">godly sorrow.</hi> Heaven will be a heaven indeed to those who go mourning thither; it will be a harvest of joy, the return of a seed-time of tears (<reference osisRef="Ps.126.5-Ps.126.6">Ps. cxxvi. 5, 6</reference>); a mountain of joy, to which our way lies through a vale of tears. See <reference osisRef="Isa.66.10">Isa. lxvi. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen21455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21456" type="x-p"/> III. <hi type="italic">The meek</hi> are happy (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.5">v. 5</reference>); <hi type="italic">Blessed are the meek.</hi> The meek are those who quietly submit themselves to God, to his word and to his rod, who follow his directions, and comply with his designs, and are <hi type="italic">gentle towards all men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.2">Tit. iii. 2</reference>); who can bear provocation without being inflamed by it; are either silent, or return a soft answer; and who can show their displeasure when there is occasion for it, without being transported into any indecencies; who can be cool when others are hot; and in their patience keep possession of their own souls, when they can scarcely keep possession of any thing else. <hi type="italic">They</hi> are the meek, who are rarely and hardly provoked, but quickly and easily pacified; and who would rather forgive twenty injuries than revenge one, having the rule of their own spirits. <div eID="gen21456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21457" type="x-p"/> These meek ones are here represented as happy, even in this world. 1. They are <hi type="italic">blessed,</hi> for they are like the blessed Jesus, in that wherein particularly they are to learn of him, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.29">ch. xi. 29</reference>. They are like the blessed God himself, who is Lord of his anger, and in whom fury is not. They are <hi type="italic">blessed,</hi> for they have the most comfortable, undisturbed enjoyment of themselves, their friends, their God; they are fit for any relation, and condition, any company; fit to live, and fit to die. 2. <hi type="italic">They shall inherit the earth;</hi> it is quoted from <reference osisRef="Ps.37.11">Ps. xxxvii. 11</reference>, and it is almost the only express temporal promise in all the New Testament. Not that they shall always have much of <hi type="italic">the earth,</hi> much less that they shall be put off with that only; but this branch of godliness has, in a special manner, <hi type="italic">the promise of life that now is.</hi> Meekness, however ridiculed and run down, has a real tendency to promote our health, wealth, comfort, and safety, even in this world. <hi type="italic">The meek</hi> and quiet are observed to live the most easy lives, compared with the froward and turbulent. Or, <hi type="italic">They shall inherit the land</hi> (so it may be read), <hi type="italic">the land of Canaan,</hi> a type of heaven. So that all the blessedness of heaven above, and all the blessings of earth beneath, are the portion of the meek. <div eID="gen21457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21458" type="x-p"/> IV. <hi type="italic">They that hunger and thirst after righteousness</hi> are happy, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.6">v. 6</reference>. Some understand this as a further instance of our outward poverty, and a low condition in this world, which not only exposes men to injury and wrong, but makes it in vain for them to seek to have justice done to them; they <hi type="italic">hunger and thirst after</hi> it, but such is the power on the side of their oppressors, that they cannot have it; they desire only that which is just and equal, but it is denied them by those that <hi type="italic">neither fear God nor regard men.</hi> This is a melancholy case! Yet, <hi type="italic">blessed are they,</hi> if they suffer these hardships for and with a good conscience; let them hope in God, who will see justice done, right take place, and will deliver the poor from their oppressors, <reference osisRef="Ps.103.6">Ps. ciii. 6</reference>. Those who contentedly bear oppression, and quietly refer themselves to God to plead their cause, shall in due time be satisfied, abundantly satisfied, in the wisdom and kindness which shall be manifested in his appearances for them. But it is certainly to be understood spiritually, of such a desire as, being terminated on such an object, is gracious, and the work of God's grace in the soul, and qualifies for the gifts of the divine favour. 1. <hi type="italic">Righteousness</hi> is here put for all spiritual blessings. See <reference osisRef="Ps.24.5">Ps. xxiv. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.6.33">ch. vi. 33</reference>. They are purchased for us by <hi type="italic">the righteousness of Christ;</hi> conveyed and secured by the imputation of that righteousness to us; and confirmed by the faithfulness of God. To have Christ <hi type="italic">made of God to us righteousness,</hi> and to be <hi type="italic">made the righteousness of God in him;</hi> to have <hi type="italic">the whole man renewed in righteousness,</hi> so as to become <hi type="italic">a new man,</hi> and to bear the image of God; to have an interest in Christ and the promises—this is <hi type="italic">righteousness.</hi> 2. These we must <hi type="italic">hunger and thirst after.</hi> We must truly and really desire them, as one who is hungry and thirsty desires meat and drink, who cannot be satisfied with any thing but meat and drink, and will be satisfied with them, though other things be wanting. Our desires of spiritual blessings must be earnest and importunate; "<hi type="italic">Give me these, or else I die;</hi> every thing else is dross and chaff, unsatisfying; give me these, and I have enough, though I had nothing else." <hi type="italic">Hunger and thirst</hi> are appetites that return frequently, and call for fresh satisfactions; so these holy desires rest not in any thing attained, but are carried out toward renewed pardons, and daily fresh supplies of grace. The quickened soul calls for constant meals of righteousness, grace to do the work of every day in its day, as duly as the living body calls for food. Those who <hi type="italic">hunger and thirst</hi> will labour for supplies; so we must not only desire spiritual blessings, but take pains for them in the use of the appointed means. Dr. Hammond, in his practical Catechism, distinguishes between <hi type="italic">hunger and thirst.</hi> <hi type="italic">Hunger</hi> is a desire of food to sustain, such as <hi type="italic">sanctifying righteousness.</hi> <hi type="italic">Thirst</hi> is the desire of drink to refresh, such as justifying <hi type="italic">righteousness,</hi> and the sense of our pardon. <div eID="gen21458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21459" type="x-p"/> Those who <hi type="italic">hunger and thirst</hi> after spiritual blessings, <hi type="italic">are blessed</hi> in those desires, and <hi type="italic">shall be filled</hi> with those blessings. (1.) They are <hi type="italic">blessed</hi> in those desires. Though all desires of grace are not grace (feigned, faint desires are not), yet such a desire as this is; it is an <hi type="italic">evidence</hi> of something <hi type="italic">good,</hi> and an <hi type="italic">earnest</hi> of something <hi type="italic">better.</hi> It is a desire of God's own raising, and he will not forsake the work of his own hands. Something or other the soul will be <hi type="italic">hungering</hi> and <hi type="italic">thirsting</hi> after; therefore <hi type="italic">they</hi> are blessed who fasten upon the right object, which is satisfying, and not deceiving; and do not <hi type="italic">pant after the dust of the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.2.7">Amos ii. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.55.2">Isa. lv. 2</reference>. (2.) They <hi type="italic">shall be filled</hi> with those blessings. God will give them what they desire to complete their satisfaction. It is God only who can <hi type="italic">fill a soul,</hi> whose grace and favour are adequate to its just desires; and he will fill those with <hi type="italic">grace for grace,</hi> who, in a sense of their own emptiness, have recourse to his fulness. He <hi type="italic">fills the hungry</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.53">Luke i. 53</reference>), <hi type="italic">satiates</hi> them, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.25">Jer. xxxi. 25</reference>. The happiness of heaven will certainly fill the soul; their righteousness shall be complete, the favour of God and his image, both in their full perfection. <div eID="gen21459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21460" type="x-p"/> V. The <hi type="italic">merciful</hi> are happy, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.7">v. 7</reference>. This, like the rest, is a paradox; for the merciful are not taken to be the wisest, nor are likely to be the richest; yet Christ pronounces them <hi type="italic">blessed.</hi> Those are the <hi type="italic">merciful,</hi> who are piously and charitably inclined to pity, help, and succour persons in misery. A man may be truly <hi type="italic">merciful,</hi> who has not wherewithal to be bountiful or liberal; and then God accepts the willing mind. We must not only bear our own afflictions patiently, but we must, by Christian sympathy, partake of the afflictions of our brethren; pity must be shown (<reference osisRef="Job.6.14">Job vi. 14</reference>), and <hi type="italic">bowels of mercy put on</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.3.12">Col. iii. 12</reference>); and, being put on, they must put forth themselves in contributing all we can for the assistance of those who are any way in misery. We must have compassion on the souls of others, and help them; pity the ignorant, and instruct them; the careless, and warn them; those who are in a state of sin, and snatch them as <hi type="italic">brands out of the burning.</hi> We must have compassion on those who are melancholy and in sorrow, and comfort them (<reference osisRef="Job.16.5">Job xvi. 5</reference>); on those whom we have advantage against, and not be rigorous and severe with them; on those who are in want, and supply them; which if we refuse to do, whatever we pretend, we <hi type="italic">shut up the bowels of our compassion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.15-Jas.2.16">James ii. 15, 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.3.17">1 John iii. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">Draw out thy soul</hi> by <hi type="italic">dealing thy bread</hi> to the hungry, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.7">Isa. lviii. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.10">10</reference>. Nay, a <hi type="italic">good man is merciful to his beast.</hi> <div eID="gen21460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21461" type="x-p"/> Now as to the merciful. 1. They are <hi type="italic">blessed;</hi> so it was said in the Old Testament; <hi type="italic">Blessed is he that considers the poor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.41.1">Ps. xli. 1</reference>. Herein they resemble God, whose goodness is his glory; in being <hi type="italic">merciful as he is merciful,</hi> we are, in our measure, <hi type="italic">perfect as he is perfect.</hi> It is an evidence of love to God; it will be a satisfaction to ourselves, to be any way instrumental for the benefit of others. One of the purest and most refined delights in this world, is that of <hi type="italic">doing good.</hi> In this word, <hi type="italic">Blessed are the merciful,</hi> is included that saying of Christ, which otherwise we find not in the gospels, <hi type="italic">It is more blessed to give than to receive,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.20.35">Acts xx. 35</reference>. 2. <hi type="italic">They shall obtain mercy;</hi> mercy <hi type="italic">with men,</hi> when they need it; <hi type="italic">he that watereth, shall be watered also himself</hi> (we know not how soon we may stand in need of kindness, and therefore should be kind); but especially mercy <hi type="italic">with God,</hi> for <hi type="italic">with the merciful he will show himself merciful,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.18.25">Ps. xviii. 25</reference>. The most <hi type="italic">merciful</hi> and charitable cannot pretend to <hi type="italic">merit,</hi> but must fly to mercy. The merciful shall find with God <hi type="italic">sparing</hi> mercy (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.14">ch. vi. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">supplying</hi> mercy (<reference osisRef="Prov.19.17">Prov. xix. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">sustaining</hi> mercy (<reference osisRef="Ps.41.2">Ps. xli. 2</reference>), mercy in that day (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.18">2 Tim. i. 18</reference>); may, they shall <hi type="italic">inherit the kingdom prepared for them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.34-Matt.25.35">ch. xxv. 34, 35</reference>); whereas <hi type="italic">they</hi> shall have <hi type="italic">judgment without mercy</hi> (which can be nothing short of <hi type="italic">hell-fire</hi>) who have <hi type="italic">shown no mercy.</hi> <div eID="gen21461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21462" type="x-p"/> VI. The <hi type="italic">pure in heart</hi> are happy (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.8">v. 8</reference>); <hi type="italic">Blessed are the poor in heart, for they shall see God.</hi> This is the most comprehensive of all the beatitudes; here holiness and happiness are fully described and put together. <div eID="gen21462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21463" type="x-p"/> 1. Here is the most <hi type="italic">comprehensive character</hi> of the blessed: they are <hi type="italic">pure in heart.</hi> Note, True religion consists in heart-purity. Those who are inwardly pure, show themselves to be under the power of <hi type="italic">pure and undefiled</hi> religion. True Christianity lies in the heart, in the <hi type="italic">purity of heart;</hi> the <hi type="italic">washing</hi> of that <hi type="italic">from wickedness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.4.14">Jer. iv. 14</reference>. We must lift up to God, not only clean hands, but a pure heart, <reference osisRef="Ps.24.4-Ps.24.5">Ps. xxiv. 4, 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.5">1 Tim. i. 5</reference>. The heart must be <hi type="italic">pure,</hi> in opposition to <hi type="italic">mixture</hi>—an honest heart that aims well; and pure, in opposition to <hi type="italic">pollution</hi> and <hi type="italic">defilement;</hi> as wine <hi type="italic">unmixed,</hi> as water <hi type="italic">unmuddied.</hi> The heart must be kept <hi type="italic">pure</hi> from <hi type="italic">fleshly lusts,</hi> all unchaste thoughts and desires; and from <hi type="italic">worldly lusts;</hi> covetousness is called <hi type="italic">filthy lucre;</hi> from all filthiness of flesh and spirit, all that which come <hi type="italic">out of the heart,</hi> and <hi type="italic">defiles the man.</hi> The heart must be <hi type="italic">purified by faith,</hi> and entire for God; must be presented and preserved a chaste virgin to Christ. <hi type="italic">Create in me such a clean heart, O God!</hi> <div eID="gen21463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21464" type="x-p"/> 2. Here is the most <hi type="italic">comprehensive comfort</hi> of the blessed; They shall see God. Note, (1.) It is the perfection of the soul's happiness to <hi type="italic">see God; seeing him,</hi> as we may by faith in our present state, is a <hi type="italic">heaven upon earth;</hi> and seeing him as we shall in the future state, in the <hi type="italic">heaven of heaven.</hi> To see him <hi type="italic">as he is,</hi> face to face, and no longer through a glass darkly; to see him as ours, and to see him and enjoy him; to see him and be like him, and be satisfied with that likeness (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.15">Ps. xvii. 15</reference>); and to see him for ever, and never lose the sight of him; this is heaven's happiness. (2.) The happiness of seeing God is promised to those, and those only, who are <hi type="italic">pure in heart.</hi> None but the <hi type="italic">pure</hi> are capable of <hi type="italic">seeing</hi> God, nor would it be a felicity to the impure. What pleasure could an unsanctified soul take in the vision of a holy God? As <hi type="italic">he</hi> cannot endure to look upon their iniquity, <hi type="italic">so they</hi> cannot endure to look upon his purity; nor shall any unclean thing enter into the new Jerusalem; but all that are <hi type="italic">pure in heart,</hi> all that are truly sanctified, have desires wrought in them, which nothing but the sight of God will sanctify; and divine grace will not leave those desires unsatisfied. <div eID="gen21464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21465" type="x-p"/> VII. The <hi type="italic">peace-makers</hi> are happy, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.9">v. 9</reference>. The wisdom that is from above is first <hi type="italic">pure,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">peaceable;</hi> the blessed ones are <hi type="italic">pure</hi> toward God, and <hi type="italic">peaceable</hi> toward men; for with reference to both, conscience must be kept <hi type="italic">void of offence.</hi> The <hi type="italic">peace-makers</hi> are those who have, 1. <hi type="italic">A peaceable disposition:</hi> as, to <hi type="italic">make a lie,</hi> is to be given and addicted to lying, so, to <hi type="italic">make peace,</hi> is to have a strong and hearty affection to peace. <hi type="italic">I am for peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.120.7">Ps. cxx. 7</reference>. It is to love, and desire, and delight in peace; to be put in it as in our element, and to study to be quiet. 2. A <hi type="italic">peaceable conversation;</hi> industriously, as far as we can, to preserve the peace that it be not broken, and to recover it when it is broken; to hearken to proposals of peace ourselves, and to be ready to make them to others; where distance is among brethren and neighbours, to do all we can to accommodate it, and to be <hi type="italic">repairers of the breaches. The making of peace</hi> is sometimes a <hi type="italic">thankless office,</hi> and it is the lot of him who parts a fray, to have <hi type="italic">blows on both sides;</hi> yet it is a good office, and we must be forward to it. Some think that this is intended especially as a lesson for ministers, who should do all they can to reconcile those who are at variance, and to promote Christian love among those under their charge. <div eID="gen21465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21466" type="x-p"/> Now, (1.) Such persons are <hi type="italic">blessed;</hi> for they have the satisfaction of <hi type="italic">enjoying themselves,</hi> by keeping the peace, and of being truly serviceable to others, by disposing them to peace. They are working together with Christ, who came into the world to <hi type="italic">slay all enmities,</hi> and to proclaim <hi type="italic">peace on earth.</hi> (2.) <hi type="italic">They shall be called the children of God;</hi> it will be an evidence to themselves that they are so; God will own them as such, and herein they will resemble him. He is the God of peace; the Son of God is the Prince of peace; the Spirit of adoption is a Spirit of peace. Since God has declared himself reconcilable to us all, he will not own those for his children who are implacable in their enmity to one another; for if the peacemakers are blessed, woe to the peace-breakers! Now by this it appears, that Christ never intended to have his religion propagated by fire and sword, or penal laws, or to acknowledge bigotry, or intemperate zeal, as the mark of his disciples. The children of this world love to fish in troubled waters, but the children of God are the peace-makers, the <hi type="italic">quiet in the land.</hi> <div eID="gen21466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21467" type="x-p"/> VIII. Those who are <hi type="italic">persecuted for righteousness' sake,</hi> are happy. This is the greatest paradox of all, and peculiar to Christianity; and therefore it is put last, and more largely insisted upon than any of the rest, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.10-Matt.5.12">v. 10-12</reference>. This beatitude, like Pharaoh's dream, is doubled, because hardly credited, and yet <hi type="italic">the thing is certain;</hi> and in the latter part there is change of the person, "Blessed are <hi type="italic">ye</hi>—ye my disciples, and immediate followers. This is that which you, who excel in virtue, are more immediately concerned in; for you must reckon upon hardships and troubles more than other men." Observe here, <div eID="gen21467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21468" type="x-p"/> 1. The case of suffering saints described; and it is a hard case, and a very piteous one. <div eID="gen21468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21469" type="x-p"/> (1.) They are persecuted, hunted, pursued, run down, as noxious beasts are, that are sought for to be destroyed; as if a Christian did <hi type="italic">caput gerere lupinum—bear a wolf's head,</hi> as an outlaw is said to do—any one that finds him may slay him; they are abandoned as the <hi type="italic">offscouring of all things;</hi> fined, imprisoned, banished, stripped of their estates, excluded from all places of profit and trust, scourged, racked, tortured, always delivered to death, and accounted as sheep for the slaughter. This has been the effect of the enmity of the serpent's seed against the holy seed, ever since the time <hi type="italic">of righteous Abel.</hi> It was so in <hi type="italic">Old-Testament</hi> times, as we find, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.35">Heb. xi. 35</reference>, &c. Christ has told us that it would much more be so with the Christian church, and we are not to think it strange, <reference osisRef="1John.3.13">1 John iii. 13</reference>. He has left us an example. <div eID="gen21469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21470" type="x-p"/> (2.) The are <hi type="italic">reviled, and have all manner of evil said against them falsely.</hi> Nicknames, and names of reproach, are fastened upon them, upon particular persons, and upon the generation of the righteous in the gross, to render them odious; sometimes to make them formidable, that they may be powerfully assailed; things are laid to their charge that they knew not, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.11">Ps. xxxv. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.20.18">Jer. xx. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.17.6">Acts xvii. 6, 7</reference>. Those who have had no power in their hands to do them any other mischief, could yet do this; and those who have had power to <hi type="italic">persecute,</hi> had found it necessary to <hi type="italic">do this too,</hi> to justify themselves in their barbarous usage of them; they could not have baited them, if they had not dressed them in bear-skins; nor have given them the worst of treatment, if they had not first represented them as the worst of men. They will <hi type="italic">revile you, and persecute you.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">Reviling</hi> the saints is <hi type="italic">persecuting</hi> them, and will be found so shortly, when <hi type="italic">hard speeches</hi> must be accounted for (<reference osisRef="Jude.1.15">Jude 15</reference>), and <hi type="italic">cruel mockings,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.11.36">Heb. xi. 36</reference>. They will say <hi type="italic">all manner of evil of you falsely;</hi> sometimes before the <hi type="italic">seat of judgment,</hi> as witnesses; sometimes in the <hi type="italic">seat of the scornful,</hi> with <hi type="italic">hypocritical mockers at feasts;</hi> they are the <hi type="italic">song of the drunkards;</hi> sometimes to face their faces, as Shimei cursed David; sometimes behind their backs, as the enemies of Jeremiah did. Note, There is no evil so black and horrid, which, at one time or other, has not been said, falsely, of Christ's disciples and followers. <div eID="gen21470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21471" type="x-p"/> (3.) All this is <hi type="italic">for righteousness' sake</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.10">v. 10</reference>); <hi type="italic">for my sake,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.5.11">v. 11</reference>. If for <hi type="italic">righteousness' sake,</hi> then for <hi type="italic">Christ's sake,</hi> for he is nearly interested in the work of righteousness. Enemies to righteousness are enemies to Christ. This precludes those from the blessedness who suffer <hi type="italic">justly,</hi> and are evil spoken of <hi type="italic">truly</hi> for their real crimes; let such be ashamed and confounded, it is part of their punishment; it is not the suffering, but the cause, that makes the martyr. Those suffer for <hi type="italic">righteousness' sake,</hi> who suffer because they will not sin against their consciences, and who suffer for doing that which is good. Whatever pretence persecutors have, it is the power of godliness that they have an enmity to; it is really Christ and his righteousness that are maligned, hated, and persecuted; <hi type="italic">For thy sake I have borne reproach,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.69.9">Ps. lxix. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.36">Rom. viii. 36</reference>. <div eID="gen21471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21472" type="x-p"/> 2. The comforts of suffering saints laid down. <div eID="gen21472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21473" type="x-p"/> (1.) They <hi type="italic">are blessed;</hi> for they now, in their life-time, receive <hi type="italic">their evil things</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.25">Luke xvi. 25</reference>), and receive them upon a good account. They are <hi type="italic">blessed;</hi> for it is an honour to them (<reference osisRef="Acts.5.41">Acts v. 41</reference>); it is an opportunity of glorifying Christ, of doing good, and of experiencing special comforts and visits of grace and tokens of his presence, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.5">2 Cor. i. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.3.25">Dan. iii. 25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.29">Rom. viii. 29</reference>. <div eID="gen21473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21474" type="x-p"/> (2.) They shall be <hi type="italic">recompensed;</hi> Theirs is <hi type="italic">the kingdom of heaven.</hi> They have at present a sure title to it, and sweet foretastes of it; and shall ere long be in possession of it. Though there be nothing in those sufferings than can, in strictness, merit of God (for the sins of the best deserve the worst), yet this is here promised as a <hi type="italic">reward</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.12">v. 12</reference>); <hi type="italic">Great is your reward in heaven:</hi> so great, as far to transcend the service. It is <hi type="italic">in heaven,</hi> future, and out of sight; but well secured, out of the reach of chance, fraud, and violence. Note, God will provide that those who lose <hi type="italic">for</hi> him, though it be life itself, shall not lose <hi type="italic">by</hi> him in the end. Heaven, at last, will be an abundant recompence for all the difficulties we meet with in our way. This is that which has borne up the suffering saints in all ages—this <hi type="italic">joy set before them.</hi> <div eID="gen21474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21475" type="x-p"/> (3.) "<hi type="italic">So persecuted they the prophets that were before you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.5.12">v. 12</reference>. They were <hi type="italic">before you</hi> in excellency, above what you are yet arrived at; they were <hi type="italic">before you</hi> in time, that they might be examples to you of <hi type="italic">suffering affliction</hi> and <hi type="italic">of patience,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.5.10">James v. 10</reference>. They were in like manner persecuted and abused; and can you expect to go to heaven in a way by yourself? Was not Isaiah mocked for his <hi type="italic">line upon line?</hi> <hi type="italic">Elisha</hi> for his <hi type="italic">bald head?</hi> Were not all the prophets thus treated? Therefore <hi type="italic">marvel not</hi> at it as a <hi type="italic">strange</hi> thing, <hi type="italic">murmur not</hi> at it as a <hi type="italic">hard</hi> thing; it is a comfort to see the way of suffering a beaten road, and an honour to follow such leaders. That grace which was <hi type="italic">sufficient for them,</hi> to carry them through their sufferings, shall not be <hi type="italic">deficient to you.</hi> Those who are your enemies are the seed and successors of them who of old mocked the messengers of the Lord," <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.16">2 Chron. xxxvi. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.23.31">ch. xxiii. 31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.7.52">Acts vii. 52</reference>.
entries.4a33b2b2015512d961609cac67b7dc6c08ddaacc: <div eID="gen21475" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sermon on the Mount.</title> <div sID="gen21476" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men. <hi type="super">14</hi> Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on a hill cannot be hid. <hi type="super">15</hi> Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house. <hi type="super">16</hi> Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven. <div eID="gen21476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21477" type="x-p"/> Christ had lately called his disciples, and told them that they should be <hi type="italic">fishers of men;</hi> here he tells them further what he designed them to be—<hi type="italic">the salt of the earth,</hi> and <hi type="italic">lights of the world,</hi> that they might be indeed what it was expected they should be. <div eID="gen21477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21478" type="x-p"/> I. <hi type="italic">Ye are the salt of the earth.</hi> <hi type="italic">This</hi> would encourage and support them under their sufferings, that, though they should be treated with contempt, yet they should really be blessings to the world, and the more so for their suffering thus. The prophets, who went before them, were the salt of the land of Canaan; but the apostles were the salt of <hi type="italic">the whole earth,</hi> for they must <hi type="italic">go into all the world to preach the gospel.</hi> It was a discouragement to them that they were so <hi type="italic">few</hi> and so <hi type="italic">weak.</hi> What could they do in so large a province as <hi type="italic">the whole earth?</hi> Nothing, if they were to work by force of arms and dint of sword; but, being to work silent as salt, one handful of that salt would diffuse its savour far and wide; would go a great way, and work insensibly and irresistibly as leaven, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.33">ch. xiii. 33</reference>. The doctrine of the gospel is as <hi type="italic">salt;</hi> it is penetrating, <hi type="italic">quick,</hi> and <hi type="italic">powerful</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.4.12">Heb. iv. 12</reference>); it reaches <hi type="italic">the heart</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.2.37">Acts ii. 37</reference>. It is cleansing, it is relishing, and preserves from putrefaction. We read of the <hi type="italic">savour of the knowledge of Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.14">2 Cor. ii. 14</reference>); for all other learning is insipid without that. An everlasting covenant is called a <hi type="italic">covenant of salt</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.18.19">Num. xviii. 19</reference>); and the gospel is an everlasting gospel. Salt was required in all the sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Lev.2.13">Lev. ii. 13</reference>), in Ezekiel's mystical temple, <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.24">Ezek. xliii. 24</reference>. Now Christ's disciples having themselves learned the doctrine of the gospel, and being employed to teach it to others, were as salt. Note, Christians, and especially ministers, are the salt of the earth. <div eID="gen21478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21479" type="x-p"/> 1. If they be as they should be they are <hi type="italic">as good salt,</hi> white, and small, and broken into many grains, but very useful and necessary. Pliny says, <hi type="italic">Sine sale, vita humana non potest degere—Without salt human life cannot be sustained.</hi> See in this, (1.) What they are to be in themselves—seasoned with the gospel, with the salt of grace; thoughts and affections, words and actions, all seasoned with grace, <reference osisRef="Col.4.6">Col. iv. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">Have salt in yourselves,</hi> else you cannot diffuse it among others, <reference osisRef="Mark.9.50">Mark ix. 50</reference>. (2.) What they are to be to others; they must not only <hi type="italic">be</hi> good but <hi type="italic">do</hi> good, must insinuate themselves into the minds of the people, not to serve any secular interest of their own, but that they might transform them into the taste and relish of the gospel. (3.) What great blessings they are to the world. Mankind, lying in ignorance and wickedness, were a vast heap of unsavoury stuff, ready to putrefy; but Christ sent forth his disciples, by their lives and doctrines, to season it with knowledge and grace, and so to render it acceptable to God, to the angels, and to all that relish divine things. (4.) How they must expect to be disposed of. They must not be laid on a heap, must not continue always together at Jerusalem, but must be scattered as salt upon the meat, here a grain and there a grain; as the Levites were dispersed in Israel, that, wherever they live, they may communicate their savour. Some have observed, that whereas it is foolishly called an ill omen to have the salt fall towards us, it is really an ill omen to have the salt fall from us. <div eID="gen21479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21480" type="x-p"/> 2. If they be not, they are as <hi type="italic">salt</hi> that has <hi type="italic">lost its savour.</hi> If you, who should season others, are yourselves unsavoury, void of spiritual life, relish, and vigour; if a Christian be so, especially if a minister be so, his condition is very sad; for, (1.) He is <hi type="italic">irrecoverable:</hi> <hi type="italic">Wherewith shall it be salted?</hi> Salt is a remedy for <hi type="italic">unsavoury meat,</hi> but there is no remedy for <hi type="italic">unsavoury salt.</hi> Christianity will give a man a relish; but if a man can take up and continue the profession of it, and yet remain flat and foolish, and graceless and insipid, no other doctrine, no other means, can be applied, to make him savoury. If Christianity do not do it, nothing will. (2.) He is <hi type="italic">unprofitable:</hi> <hi type="italic">It is thenceforth good for nothing;</hi> what use can it be put to, in which it will not do more hurt than good? As a man without reason, so is a Christian without grace. A wicked man is the worst of creatures; a wicked Christian is the worst of men; and a wicked minister is the worst of Christians. (3.) He is doomed to ruin and rejection; He shall be <hi type="italic">cast out</hi>—expelled the church and the communion of the faithful, to which he is a blot and a burden; and he shall be <hi type="italic">trodden under foot of men.</hi> Let God be glorified in the shame and rejection of those by whom he has been reproached, and who have made themselves fit for nothing but to be trampled upon. <div eID="gen21480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21481" type="x-p"/> II. <hi type="italic">Ye are the light of the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.5.14">v. 14</reference>. This also bespeaks them useful, as the former (<hi type="italic">Sole et sale nihil utilius—Nothing more useful than the sun and salt</hi>), but more glorious. All Christians are <hi type="italic">light in the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.8">Eph. v. 8</reference>), and must <hi type="italic">shine as lights</hi> (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.15">Phil. ii. 15</reference>), but ministers in a special manner. Christ call himself <hi type="italic">the Light of the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.8.12">John viii. 12</reference>), and they are <hi type="italic">workers together with him,</hi> and have some of his honour put upon them. Truly <hi type="italic">the light is sweet,</hi> it is welcome; the light of the first day of the world was so, when it <hi type="italic">shone out of darkness;</hi> so is the morning light of every day; so is the gospel, and those that spread it, to all sensible people. The <hi type="italic">world sat in darkness,</hi> Christ raised up his disciples to shine in it; and, that they may do so, from him they borrow and derive their light. <div eID="gen21481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21482" type="x-p"/> This similitude is here explained in two things: <div eID="gen21482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21483" type="x-p"/> 1. As <hi type="italic">the lights of the world,</hi> they are illustrious and conspicuous, and have many eyes upon them. A city that is <hi type="italic">set on a hill cannot be hid.</hi> The disciples of Christ, especially those who are forward and zealous in his service, become remarkable, and are taken notice of as beacons. They are for <hi type="italic">signs</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.18">Isa. vii. 18</reference>), <hi type="italic">men wondered at</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.8">Zech. iii. 8</reference>); all their neighbours have any eye upon them. Some admire them, commend them, rejoice in them, and study to imitate them; others envy them, hate them, censure them, and study to blast them. They are concerned therefore to <hi type="italic">walk circumspectly,</hi> because of <hi type="italic">their observers;</hi> they are as <hi type="italic">spectacles to the world,</hi> and must take heed of every thing that <hi type="italic">looks ill,</hi> because they are so much <hi type="italic">looked at.</hi> The disciples of Christ were obscure men before he called them, but the character he put upon them dignified them, and as preachers of the gospel they made a figure; and though they were reproached for it by some, they were respected for it by others, advanced to thrones, and made judges (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.30">Luke xxii. 30</reference>); for Christ will honour those that honour him. <div eID="gen21483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21484" type="x-p"/> 2. As the <hi type="italic">lights of the world,</hi> they are intended to illuminate and give light to others (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.15">v. 15</reference>), and therefore, (1.) They shall be <hi type="italic">set up</hi> as lights. Christ has lighted these candles, they shall not be put under a bushel, not confined always, as they are now, to the cities of Galilee, or the lost sheep of the house of Israel, but they shall be sent into all the world. The churches are the candlesticks, the golden candlesticks, in which these lights are placed, that they light may be diffused; and the gospel is so strong a light, and carries with it so much of its own evidence, that, <hi type="italic">like a city on a hill, it cannot be hid,</hi> it cannot but appear to be from God, to all those who do not wilfully shut their eyes against it. It will <hi type="italic">give light to all that are in the house,</hi> to all that will draw near to it, and come where it is. Those to whom it does not give light, must thank themselves; they will not be in the house with it; will not make a diligent and impartial enquiry into it, but are prejudiced against it. (2.) They must <hi type="italic">shine</hi> as lights, [1.] By their <hi type="italic">good preaching.</hi> The knowledge they have, they must communicate for the good of others; not put it <hi type="italic">under a bushel,</hi> but spread it. The talent must not be buried in a napkin, but traded with. The disciples of Christ must not muffle themselves up in privacy and obscurity, under pretence of contemplation, modesty, or self-preservation, but, <hi type="italic">as they have received the gift,</hi> must <hi type="italic">minister the same,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.3">Luke xii. 3</reference>. [2.] By their <hi type="italic">good living.</hi> They must be <hi type="italic">burning and shining lights</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.5.35">John v. 35</reference>); must evidence, in their whole conversation, that they are indeed followers of Christ, <reference osisRef="Jas.3.13">James iii. 13</reference>. They must be to others for instruction, direction, quickening, and comfort, <reference osisRef="Job.29.11">Job xxix. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen21484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21485" type="x-p"/> See here, <hi type="italic">First, How</hi> our light must shine—by doing such <hi type="italic">good works</hi> as men <hi type="italic">may see,</hi> and may approve of; such works as are of <hi type="italic">good report</hi> among them that are without, and as will therefore give them cause to think well of Christianity. We must do good works <hi type="italic">that may be seen</hi> to the edification of others, but not <hi type="italic">that they may be seen</hi> to our own ostentation; we are bid to pray in secret, and what lies between God and our souls, must be kept to ourselves; but that which is of itself open and obvious to the sight of men, we must study to make <hi type="italic">congruous</hi> to our profession, and praiseworthy, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.8">Phil. iv. 8</reference>. Those about us must not only <hi type="italic">hear</hi> our good words, but <hi type="italic">see</hi> our good works; that they may be convinced that religion is more than a bare name, and that we do not only make a profession of it, but abide under the power of it. <div eID="gen21485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21486" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> For what <hi type="italic">end</hi> our light must shine—"That those who see your good works may be brought, not to glorify <hi type="italic">you</hi> (which was the things the Pharisees aimed at, and it spoiled all their performances), but to <hi type="italic">glorify your Father which is in heaven.</hi>" Note, The glory of God is the great thing we must aim at in every thing we do in religion, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.11">1 Pet. iv. 11</reference>. In this centre the lines of all our actions must meet. We must not only endeavor to glorify God ourselves, but we must do all we can to bring others to glorify him. The sight of our <hi type="italic">good works</hi> will do this, by furnishing them, 1. With <hi type="italic">matter for praise.</hi> "Let them see <hi type="italic">your good works,</hi> that they may see the power of God's grace in you, and may thank him for it, and give him the glory of it, who has given such power unto men." 2. With <hi type="italic">motives of piety.</hi> "Let them see your good works, that they may be convinced of the truth and excellency of the Christian religion, may be provoked by a holy emulation to imitate your good works, and so may glorify God." Note, The holy, regular, and exemplary conversation of the saints, may do much towards the conversion of sinners; those who are unacquainted with religion, may hereby be brought to know what it is. Examples teach. And those who are prejudiced against it, may hereby by brought in love with it, and thus there is a winning virtue in a godly conversation.
entries.2e3bc982cae7e02562be62e854647b9401114e3f: <div eID="gen21486" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sermon on the Mount.</title> <div sID="gen21487" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil. <hi type="super">18</hi> For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled. <hi type="super">19</hi> Whosoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so, he shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven: but whosoever shall do and teach <hi type="italic">them,</hi> the same shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven. <hi type="super">20</hi> For I say unto you, That except your righteousness shall exceed <hi type="italic">the righteousness</hi> of the scribes and Pharisees, ye shall in no case enter into the kingdom of heaven. <div eID="gen21487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21488" type="x-p"/> Those to whom Christ preached, and for whose use he gave these instructions to his disciples, were such as in their religion had an eye, 1. To the <hi type="italic">scriptures</hi> of the <hi type="italic">Old Testament</hi> as their rule, and therein Christ here shows them they were in the right: 2. To the scribes and the Pharisees as their <hi type="italic">example,</hi> and therein Christ here shows them they were in the wrong; for, <div eID="gen21488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21489" type="x-p"/> I. The rule which Christ came to establish exactly agreed with the scriptures of the Old Testament, here called <hi type="italic">the law</hi> and <hi type="italic">the prophets.</hi> The <hi type="italic">prophets</hi> were commentators upon the law, and both together made up that rule of faith and practice which Christ found upon the throne in the Jewish church, and here he keeps it on the throne. <div eID="gen21489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21490" type="x-p"/> 1. He protests against the thought of cancelling and weakening the <hi type="italic">Old Testament;</hi> <hi type="italic">Think not that I am come to destroy the law and the prophets.</hi> (1.) "Let not the pious Jews, who have an affection for the <hi type="italic">law and the prophets, fear</hi> that I come to <hi type="italic">destroy</hi> them." Let them be not prejudiced against Christ and his doctrine, from a jealousy that this kingdom he came to set up, would derogate from the honour of the scriptures, which they had embraced as coming from God, and of which they had experienced the power and purity; no, let them be satisfied that Christ has no ill design upon the law and the prophets. "Let not the profane Jews, who have a disaffection to the law and the prophets, and are weary of that yoke, hope that I am come to destroy them." Let not carnal libertines imagine that the Messiah is come to discharge them from the obligation of divine precepts and yet to secure to them divine promises, to make the happy and yet to give them leave to live as they list. Christ commands nothing now which was forbidden either by the law of nature or the moral law, nor forbids any thing which those laws had enjoined; it is a great mistake to think he does, and he here takes care to rectify the mistake; <hi type="italic">I am not come to destroy.</hi> The Saviour of souls is the <hi type="italic">destroyer</hi> of nothing but the <hi type="italic">works of the devil,</hi> of nothing that comes from God, much less of those excellent dictates which we have from Moses and the prophets. No, he came to <hi type="italic">fulfil</hi> them. That is, [1.] To obey the commands of the law, for he was <hi type="italic">made under the law,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.4.4">Gal. iv. 4</reference>. He in all respects yielded obedience to the law, honoured his parents, sanctified the sabbath, prayed, gave alms, and did that which never any one else did, obeyed perfectly, and never broke the law in any thing. [2.] To make good the promises of the law, and the predictions of the prophets, which did all bear witness to him. The covenant of grace is, for substance, the same now that it was then, and Christ the Mediator of it. [3.] To answer the types of the law; thus (as bishop Tillotson expresses it), he did not make <hi type="italic">void,</hi> but make <hi type="italic">good,</hi> the ceremonial law, and manifested himself to be the Substance of all those shadows. [4.] To fill up the defects of it, and so to complete and perfect it. Thus the word <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">plerosai</hi></hi> properly signifies. If we consider the law as a vessel that had some water in it before, he did not come to pour out the water, but to fill the vessel up to the brim; or, as a picture that is first rough-drawn, displays some outlines only of the piece intended, which are afterwards filled up; so Christ made an improvement of the law and the prophets by his additions and explications. [5.] To carry on the same design; the Christian institutes are so far from thwarting and contradicting that which was the main design of the Jewish religion, that they promote it to the highest degree.
