The gospel is the <hi type="italic">time of reformation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.10">Heb. ix. 10</reference>), not the repeal of the law, but the amendment of it, and, consequently, its establishment. <div eID="gen21490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21491" type="x-p"/> 2. He asserts the perpetuity of it; that not only he designed not the abrogation of it, but that it never should be abrogated (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.18">v. 18</reference>); "<hi type="italic">Verily I say unto you,</hi> I, the <hi type="italic">Amen,</hi> the faithful Witness, solemnly declare it, that <hi type="italic">till heaven and earth pass,</hi> when time shall be no more, and the unchangeable state of recompences shall supersede all laws, <hi type="italic">one jot, or one tittle,</hi> the least and most minute circumstance, <hi type="italic">shall in no wise pass from the law till all be fulfilled;</hi>" for what is it that God is doing in all the operations both of providence and grace, but fulfilling the scripture? Heaven and earth shall come together, and all the fulness thereof be wrapped up in ruin and confusion, rather than any word of God shall fall to the ground, or be in vain. <hi type="italic">The word of the Lord endures for ever,</hi> both that of the law, and that of the gospel. Observe, The care of God concerning his law extends itself even to those things that seem to be of least account in it, the iotas and the tittles; for whatever belongs to God, and bears his stamp, be it ever so little, shall be preserved. The laws of men are conscious to themselves of so much imperfection, that they allow it for a maxim, <hi type="italic">Apices juris non sunt jura—The extreme points of the law are not the law,</hi> but God will stand by and maintain every iota and every tittle of his law. <div eID="gen21491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21492" type="x-p"/> 3. He gives it in charge to his disciples, carefully to preserve the law, and shows them the danger of the neglect and contempt of it (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.19">v. 19</reference>); <hi type="italic">Whosoever therefore shall break one of the least commandments of the law of Moses,</hi> much more any of the greater, as the Pharisees did, who neglected the weightier matters of the law, and shall teach men so as they did, who made void the commandment of God with their traditions (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.3">ch. xv. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">he shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven.</hi> Though the Pharisees be cried up for such teachers as should be, they shall not be employed as teachers in Christ's kingdom; but <hi type="italic">whosoever shall do and teach them,</hi> as Christ's disciples would, and thereby prove themselves better friends to the <hi type="italic">Old Testament</hi> than the Pharisees were, they, though despised by men, shall be <hi type="italic">called great in the kingdom of heaven.</hi> Note, (1.) Among the commands of God there are some less than others; none absolutely little, but comparatively so. The Jews reckon the least of the commandments of the law to be that of the bird's nest (<reference osisRef="Deut.22.6-Deut.22.7">Deut. xxii. 6, 7</reference>); yet even that had a significance and an intention very great and considerable. (2.) It is a dangerous thing, in doctrine or practice, to disannul the least of God's commands; to break them, that is, to go about either to <hi type="italic">contract the extent,</hi> or <hi type="italic">weaken the obligation</hi> of them; whoever does so, will find it is at his peril. Thus to vacate any of the ten commandments, is too bold a stroke for the jealous God to pass by. It is something more than transgressing the law, it is making void the law, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.126">Ps. cxix. 126</reference>. (3.) That the further such corruptions as they spread, the worse they are. It is impudence enough to break the command, but is a greater degree of it to teach men so. This plainly refers to those who at this time sat in Moses' seat, and by their comments corrupted and perverted the text. Opinions that tend to the destruction of serious godliness and the vitals of religion, by corrupt glosses on the scripture, are bad when they are held, but worse when they are propagated and taught, as the word of God. He that does so, shall be called <hi type="italic">least in the kingdom of heaven,</hi> in the kingdom of glory; he shall never come thither, but be eternally excluded; or, rather, in the kingdom of the gospel-church. He is so far from deserving the dignity of a teacher in it, that he shall not so much as be accounted a member of it. The prophet that teaches these lies shall be the tail in that kingdom (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.15">Isa. ix. 15</reference>); when truth shall appear in its own evidence, such corrupt teachers, though cried up as the Pharisees, shall be of no account with the wise and good. Nothing makes ministers more contemptible and base than corrupting the law, <reference osisRef="Mal.2.8">Mal. ii. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mal.2.11">11</reference>. Those who extenuate and encourage sin, and discountenance and put contempt upon strictness in religion and serious devotion, are the dregs of the church. But, on the other hand, Those are truly honourable, and of great account in the church of Christ, who lay out themselves by their life and doctrine to promote the purity and strictness of practical religion; who both do and teach that which is good; for those who do not as they teach, pull down with one hand what they build up with the other, and give themselves the lie, and tempt men to think that all religion is a delusion; but those who speak from experience, who live up to what they preach, are truly great; they honour God, and God will honour them (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.30">1 Sam. ii. 30</reference>), and hereafter they shall shine as the <hi type="italic">stars in the kingdom of our Father.</hi> <div eID="gen21492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21493" type="x-p"/> II. The righteousness which Christ came to establish by this rule, must exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.20">v. 20</reference>. This was strange doctrine to those who looked upon the scribes and Pharisees as having arrived at the highest pitch of religion. The scribes were the most noted teachers of the law, and the Pharisees the most celebrated professors of it, and they both sat in Moses' chair (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.2">ch. xxiii. 2</reference>), and had such a reputation among the people, that they were looked upon as super-conformable to the law, and people did not think themselves obliged to be as good as they; it was therefore a great surprise to them, to hear that they must be better than they, or they should not go to heaven; and therefore Christ here avers it with solemnity; <hi type="italic">I say unto you,</hi> It is so. The scribes and Pharisees were enemies to Christ and his doctrine, and were great oppressors; and yet it must be owned, that there was something commendable in them. They were much in fasting and prayer, and giving of alms; they were punctual in observing the ceremonial appointments, and made it their business to teach others; they had such an interest in the people that they ought, if but two men went to heaven, one would be a Pharisee; and yet our Lord Jesus here tells his disciples, that the religion he came to establish, did not only exclude the badness, but excel the goodness, of the scribes and Pharisees. We must do more than they, and better than they, or we shall come short of heaven. They were <hi type="italic">partial in the law,</hi> and laid most stress upon the ritual part of it; but we must be <hi type="italic">universal,</hi> and not think it enough to give the priest his tithe, but must give God our hearts. They minded only the <hi type="italic">outside,</hi> but we must make conscience of <hi type="italic">inside</hi> godliness. They aimed at the <hi type="italic">praise</hi> and <hi type="italic">applause of men,</hi> but we must aim at <hi type="italic">acceptance with God:</hi> they were <hi type="italic">proud</hi> of what they did in religion, and trusted to it as a <hi type="italic">righteousness;</hi> but we, when we have done all, must <hi type="italic">deny ourselves,</hi> and say, We are <hi type="italic">unprofitable servants,</hi> and trust only to the <hi type="italic">righteousness of Christ;</hi> and thus we may go beyond the scribes and Pharisees.
entries.df7ab66ce176d65fc33bb4c29688a7b0b6f68fd6: <div eID="gen21493" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sermon on the Mount.</title> <div sID="gen21494" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not kill; and whosoever shall kill shall be in danger of the judgment: <hi type="super">22</hi> But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire. <hi type="super">23</hi> Therefore if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee; <hi type="super">24</hi> Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift. <hi type="super">25</hi> Agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him; lest at any time the adversary deliver thee to the judge, and the judge deliver thee to the officer, and thou be cast into prison. <hi type="super">26</hi> Verily I say unto thee, Thou shalt by no means come out thence, till thou hast paid the uttermost farthing. <div eID="gen21494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21495" type="x-p"/> Christ having laid down these principles, that Moses and the prophets were still to be their rulers, but that the scribes and Pharisees were to be no longer their rulers, proceeds to expound the law in some particular instances, and to vindicate it from the corrupt glosses which those expositors had put upon it. He adds not any thing new, only limits and restrains some permissions which had been abused: and as to the precepts, shows the breadth, strictness, and spiritual nature of them, adding such explanatory statutes as made them more clear, and tended much toward the perfecting of our obedience to them. In these verses, he explains the law of the sixth commandment, according to the true intent and full extent of it. <div eID="gen21495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21496" type="x-p"/> I. Here is the <hi type="italic">command itself</hi> laid down (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.12">v. 12</reference>); <hi type="italic">We have heard it,</hi> and remember it; he speaks <hi type="italic">to them who know the law,</hi> who had Moses read to them in their synagogues every sabbath-day; you have heard that it was said <hi type="italic">by them,</hi> or rather as it is in the margin, <hi type="italic">to them of old time,</hi> to your forefathers the Jews, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not kill.</hi> Note, The laws of God are not novel, upstart laws, but were delivered to them of old time; they are ancient laws, but of that nature as never to be <hi type="italic">antiquated</hi> nor grow <hi type="italic">obsolete.</hi> The moral law agrees with the law of nature, and the eternal rules and reasons of good and evil, that is, the rectitude of the eternal Mind. <hi type="italic">Killing</hi> is here forbidden, killing ourselves, killing any other, directly or indirectly, or being any way accessory to it. The law of God, the God of life, is a hedge of protection about our lives. It was one of the precepts of Noah, <reference osisRef="Gen.9.5-Gen.9.6">Gen. ix. 5, 6</reference>. <div eID="gen21496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21497" type="x-p"/> II. The exposition of this command which the Jewish teachers contended themselves with; their comment upon it was, <hi type="italic">Whosoever shall kill, shall be in danger of the judgment.</hi> This was all they had to say upon it, that wilful murderers were liable to the sword of justice, and casual ones to the judgment of the city of refuge. The courts of judgment sat in the gate of their principal cities; the judges, ordinarily, were in number twenty-three; these tried, condemned, and executed murderers; so that whoever killed, was in danger of their judgment. Now this gloss of theirs upon this commandment was faulty, for it intimated, 1. That the law of the sixth commandment was only external, and forbade no more than the act of murder, and laid to restraint upon the inward lusts, from which <hi type="italic">wars and fightings come.</hi> This was indeed the <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">proton pseudos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the fundamental error</hi> of the Jewish teachers, that the divine law prohibited only the sinful act, not the sinful thought; they were disposed <hi type="italic">hærere in cortice—to rest in the letter</hi> of the law, and they never enquired into the spiritual meaning of it. Paul, while a Pharisee, did not, till, by the key of the tenth commandment, divine grace let him into the knowledge of the spiritual nature of all the rest, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.7">Rom. vii. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.14">14</reference>. 2. Another mistake of theirs was, that this law was merely <hi type="italic">political</hi> and <hi type="italic">municipal,</hi> given for them, and intended as a directory for their courts, and no more; as if they only were the people, and the wisdom of the law must die with them. <div eID="gen21497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21498" type="x-p"/> III. The exposition which Christ gave of this commandment; and we are sure that according to his exposition of it we must be judged hereafter, and therefore ought to be ruled now. <hi type="italic">The commandment is exceeding broad,</hi> and not to be limited by the will of the flesh, or the will of men. <div eID="gen21498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21499" type="x-p"/> 1. Christ tells them that <hi type="italic">rash anger is heart-murder</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.22">v. 22</reference>); <hi type="italic">Whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause,</hi> breaks the sixth commandment. By our <hi type="italic">brother</hi> here, we are to understand any person, though ever so much our inferior, as a child, a servant, for we are all <hi type="italic">made of one blood.</hi> Anger is a natural passion; there are cases in which it is lawful and laudable; but it is then <hi type="italic">sinful,</hi> when we are angry without cause. The word is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eike</hi></hi>, which signifies, <hi type="italic">sine caus&#226;, sine effectu, et sine modo—without cause, without any good effect, without moderation;</hi> so that the anger is then sinful, (1.) When it is without any just provocation given; either for no cause, or no good cause, or no great and proportionable cause; when we are angry at children or servants for that which could not be helped, which was only a piece of forgetfulness or mistake, that we ourselves might easily have been guilty of, and for which we should not have been angry at ourselves; when we are angry upon groundless surmises, or for trivial affronts not worth speaking of. (2.) When it is without any good end aimed at, merely to show our authority, to gratify a brutish passion, to let people know our resentments, and excite ourselves to revenge, then it is in vain, it is to do hurt; whereas if we are at any time angry, it should be to awaken the offender to repentance, and prevent his doing so again; to clear ourselves (<reference osisRef="2Cor.7.11">2 Cor. vii. 11</reference>), and to give warning to others. (3.) When it exceeds due bounds; when we are hardy and headstrong in our anger, violent and vehement, outrageous and mischievous, and when we seek the hurt of those we are displeased at. This is a breach of the sixth commandment, for he that is thus angry, would kill if he could and durst; he has taken the first step toward it; Cain's killing his brother began in anger; he is a murderer in the account of God, who knows his heart, whence murder proceeds, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.19">ch. xv. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen21499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21500" type="x-p"/> 2. He tells them, that given opprobrious language to our brother is tongue-murder, calling him, <hi type="italic">Raca,</hi> and, <hi type="italic">Thou fool.</hi> When this is done with mildness and for a good end, to convince others of their vanity and folly, it is not sinful. Thus James says, <hi type="italic">O vain man;</hi> and Paul, <hi type="italic">Thou fool;</hi> and Christ himself, <hi type="italic">O fools, and slow of heart.</hi> But when it proceeds from anger and malice within, it is the smoke of that fire which is kindled from hell, and falls under the same character. (1.) <hi type="italic">Raca</hi> is a scornful word, and comes from pride, "Thou empty fellow;" it is the language of that which Solomon calls <hi type="italic">proud wrath</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.21.24">Prov. xxi. 24</reference>), which tramples upon our brother-disdains <hi type="italic">to set him even with the dogs of our flock. This people who knoweth not the law, is cursed,</hi> is such language, <reference osisRef="John.7.49">John vii. 49</reference>. (2.) <hi type="italic">Thou fool,</hi> is a spiteful word, and comes from hatred; looking upon him, not only as mean and not to be honoured, but as vile and not to be loved; "Thou wicked man, thou reprobate." The former speaks a man without sense, this (in scripture language) speaks a man without grace; the more the reproach touches his spiritual condition, the worse it is; the former is a haughty taunting of our brother, this is a malicious censuring and condemning of him, as abandoned of God. Now this is a breach of the sixth commandment; malicious slanders and censures are <hi type="italic">poison under the tongue,</hi> that kills secretly and slowly; <hi type="italic">bitter words</hi> are as <hi type="italic">arrows</hi> that would suddenly (<reference osisRef="Ps.64.3">Ps. lxiv. 3</reference>), or as a sword in the bones. The good name of our neighbour, which is better than life, is thereby stabbed and murdered; and it is an evidence of such an ill-will to our neighbour as would strike at his life, if it were in our power. <div eID="gen21500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21501" type="x-p"/> 3. He tells them, that how light soever they made of these sins, they would certainly be reckoned for; he <hi type="italic">that is angry with is brother shall be in danger of the judgment</hi> and anger of God; he that calls him <hi type="italic">Raca, shall be in danger of the council,</hi> of being punished by the Sanhedrim for reviling an Israelite; <hi type="italic">but whosoever saith, Thou fool,</hi> thou profane person, thou child of hell, <hi type="italic">shall be in danger of hell-fire,</hi> to which he condemns his brother; so the learned Dr. Whitby. Some think, in allusion to the penalties used in the several courts of judgment among the Jews, Christ shows that the sin of rash anger exposes men to lower or higher punishments, according to the degrees of its proceeding. The Jews had three capital punishments, each worse than the other; beheading, which was inflicted by the judgment; stoning, by the council or chief Sanhedrim; and burning <hi type="italic">in the valley of the son of Hinnom,</hi> which was used only in extraordinary cases: it signifies, therefore, that rash anger and reproachful language are damning sins; but some are more sinful than others, and accordingly there is a greater damnation, and a sorer punishment reserved for them: Christ would thus show which sin was most sinful, by showing which it was the punishment whereof was most dreadful. <div eID="gen21501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21502" type="x-p"/> IV. From all this it is here inferred, that we ought carefully to preserve Christian love and peace with our brethren, and that if at any time a breach happens, we should labour for a reconciliation, by confessing our fault, humbling ourselves to our brother, begging his pardon, and making restitution, or offering satisfaction for wrong done in word or deed, according as the nature of the thing is; and that we should do this quickly for two reasons: <div eID="gen21502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21503" type="x-p"/> 1. Because, till this be done, we are utterly unfit for communion with God in holy ordinances, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.23-Matt.5.24">v. 23, 24</reference>. The case supposed is, "<hi type="italic">That thy brother have</hi> somewhat <hi type="italic">against thee,</hi>" that thou has injured and offended him, either really or in his apprehension; if thou are the party offended, there needs not this delay; if thou <hi type="italic">have aught against thy brother,</hi> make short work of it; no more is to be done but to forgive him (<reference osisRef="Mark.11.25">Mark xi. 25</reference>), and forgive the injury; but if the quarrel began on thy side, and the fault was either at first or afterwards thine, so <hi type="italic">that thy brother</hi> has a controversy with <hi type="italic">thee, go</hi> and <hi type="italic">be reconciled to</hi> him before thou <hi type="italic">offer thy gift at the altar,</hi> before thou approach solemnly to God in the gospel-services of prayer and praise, hearing the word or the sacraments. Note, (1.) When we are addressing ourselves to any religious exercises, it is good for us to take that occasion of serious reflection and self-examination: there are many things to be <hi type="italic">remembered,</hi> when we <hi type="italic">bring our gift to the altar,</hi> and this among the rest, whether <hi type="italic">our brother hath aught against us;</hi> then, if ever, we are disposed to be serious, and therefore should then call ourselves to an account. (2.) Religious exercises are not acceptable to God, if they are performed when we are in wrath; envy, malice, and uncharitableness, are sins so displeasing to God, that nothing pleases him which comes from a heart wherein they are predominant, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.8">1 Tim. ii. 8</reference>. Prayers made in wrath are written in gall, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.15">Isa. i. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.4">lviii. 4</reference>. (3.) Love or charity is so much <hi type="italic">better than all burnt-offerings and sacrifice,</hi> that God will have reconciliation made with an offended brother before the gift be offered; he is content to stay for the gift, rather than have it offered while we are under guilt and engaged in a quarrel. (4.) Though we are unfitted for communion with God, by a continual quarrel with a brother, yet that can be no excuse for the omission or neglect of our duty: "<hi type="italic">Leave there thy gift before the altar,</hi> lest otherwise, when thou has gone away, thou be tempted not to come again." Many give this as a reason why they do not come to church or to the communion, because they are at variance with some neighbour; and whose fault is that? One sin will never excuse another, but will rather double the guilt. Want of charity cannot justify the want of piety. The difficulty is easily got over; those who have wronged us, we must forgive; and those whom we have wronged, we must make satisfaction to, or at least make a tender of it, and desire a renewal of the friendship, so that if reconciliation be not made, it may not be our fault; <hi type="italic">and then come,</hi> come and welcome, <hi type="italic">come and offer thy gift,</hi> and it shall be accepted. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> we must <hi type="italic">not let the sun go down upon our wrath</hi> any day, because we must go to prayer before we go to sleep; much less let the sun rise <hi type="italic">upon our wrath</hi> on a sabbath-day, because it is a day of prayer. <div eID="gen21503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21504" type="x-p"/> 2. Because, till this be done, we lie exposed to much danger, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.25-Matt.5.26">v. 25, 26</reference>. It is at our peril if we do not labour after an agreement, and that quickly, upon two accounts: <div eID="gen21504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21505" type="x-p"/> (1.) Upon a temporal account. If the offence we have done to our brother, in his body, goods, or reputation, be such as will bear action, in which he may recover considerable damages, it is our wisdom, and it is our duty to our family, to prevent that by a humble submission and a just and peaceable satisfaction; lest otherwise he recover it by law, and put us to the extremity of a prison. In such a case it is better to compound and make the best terms we can, than to stand it out; for it is in vain to contend with the law, and there is danger of our being crushed by it. Many ruin their estates by an obstinate persisting in the offences they have given, which would soon have been pacified by a little yielding at first. Solomon's advice in case of suretyship is, <hi type="italic">Go, humble thyself,</hi> and so secure <hi type="italic">and deliver thyself,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.6.1-Prov.6.5">Prov. vi. 1-5</reference>. It is good to agree, for the law is costly. Though we must be merciful to those we have advantage against, yet we must be just to those that have advantage against us, as far as we are able. "<hi type="italic">Agree,</hi> and compound <hi type="italic">with thine adversary quickly,</hi> lest he be exasperated by thy stubbornness, and provoked to insist upon the utmost demand, and will not make thee the abatement which at first he would have made." A prison is an uncomfortable place to those who are brought to it by their own pride and prodigality, their own wilfulness and folly. <div eID="gen21505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21506" type="x-p"/> (2.) Upon a spiritual account. "<hi type="italic">Go,</hi> and be <hi type="italic">reconciled to thy brother,</hi> be just to him, be friendly with him, because while the quarrel continues, as thou art unfit to <hi type="italic">bring thy gift to the altar,</hi> unfit to come to <hi type="italic">the table of the Lord,</hi> so thou art unfit to die: if thou persist in this sin, there is danger lest thou be suddenly snatched away by the wrath of God, whose judgment thou canst not escape nor except against; and if that iniquity be laid to thy charge, thou art undone for ever." Hell is a prison for all that live and die in malice and uncharitableness, for all that are <hi type="italic">contentious</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.8">Rom. ii. 8</reference>), and out of that prison there is no rescue, no redemption, no escape, to eternity. <div eID="gen21506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21507" type="x-p"/> This is very applicable to the great business of our reconciliation to God through Christ; <hi type="italic">Agree with him quickly, whilst thou art in the way.</hi> Note, [1.] The great God is an Adversary to all sinners, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Antidikos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">a law-adversary;</hi> he has a controversy with them, an action against them. [2.] It is our concern to <hi type="italic">agree with him,</hi> to acquaint ourselves with him, that we may <hi type="italic">be at peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.22.21">Job xxii. 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.20">2 Cor. v. 20</reference>. [3.] It is our wisdom to do this <hi type="italic">quickly, while we are in the way.</hi> While we are alive, <hi type="italic">we are in the way;</hi> after death, it will be too late to do it; therefore <hi type="italic">give not sleep to thine eyes</hi> till it be done. [4.] They who continue in a state of enmity to God, are continually exposed to the arrests of his justice, and the most dreadful instances of his wrath. Christ is the Judge, to whom impenitent sinners will be delivered; for <hi type="italic">all judgment is committed to the Son;</hi> he that was rejected as a Saviour, cannot be escaped as a Judge, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.16-Rev.6.17">Rev. vi. 16, 17</reference>. It is a fearful thing to be thus turned over to the Lord Jesus, when the Lamb shall become the Lion. Angels are the officers to whom Christ will deliver them (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.41-Matt.13.42">ch. xiii. 41, 42</reference>); devils are so too, having <hi type="italic">the power of death</hi> as executioners to all unbelievers, <reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">Heb. ii. 14</reference>. Hell is the prison, into which those will be cast that continue in a state of enmity to God, <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.4">2 Pet. ii. 4</reference>. [5.] Damned sinners must remain in it to eternity; they shall not <hi type="italic">depart till they have paid the uttermost farthing,</hi> and that will not be to the utmost ages of eternity: divine justice will be for ever in the satisfying, but never satisfied.
entries.1182bfdebf2416c5632fddc58cb348ac5e890d87: <div eID="gen21507" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sermon on the Mount.</title> <div sID="gen21508" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery: <hi type="super">28</hi> But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart. <hi type="super">29</hi> And if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast <hi type="italic">it</hi> from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not <hi type="italic">that</hi> thy whole body should be cast into hell. <hi type="super">30</hi> And if thy right hand offend thee, cut it off, and cast <hi type="italic">it</hi> from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not <hi type="italic">that</hi> thy whole body should be cast into hell. <hi type="super">31</hi> It hath been said, Whosoever shall put away his wife, let him give her a writing of divorcement: <hi type="super">32</hi> But I say unto you, That whosoever shall put away his wife, saving for the cause of fornication, causeth her to commit adultery: and whosoever shall marry her that is divorced committeth adultery. <div eID="gen21508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21509" type="x-p"/> We have here an exposition of the seventh commandment, given us by the same hand that made the law, and therefore was fittest to be the interpreter of it: it is the law against uncleanness, which fitly follows upon the former; <hi type="italic">that</hi> laid a restraint upon sinful passions, <hi type="italic">this</hi> upon sinful appetites, both which ought always to be under the government of reason and conscience, and if indulged, are equally pernicious. <div eID="gen21509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21510" type="x-p"/> I. The command is here laid down (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.27">v. 27</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not commit adultery;</hi> which includes a prohibition of all other acts of uncleanness, and the desire of them: but the Pharisees, in their expositions of this command, made it to extend no further than the act of adultery, suggesting, that if the iniquity was only <hi type="italic">regarded in the heart,</hi> and went no further, God could not hear it, would not regard it (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.18">Ps. lxvi. 18</reference>), and therefore they thought it enough to be able to say that they were <hi type="italic">no adulterers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.18.11">Luke xviii. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen21510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21511" type="x-p"/> II. It is here explained in the strictness of it, in three things, which would seem new and strange to those who had been always governed by the tradition of the elders, and took all for oracular that they taught. <div eID="gen21511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21512" type="x-p"/> 1. We are here taught, that there is such a thing as <hi type="italic">heart-adultery,</hi> adulterous thoughts and dispositions, which never proceed to the act of adultery or fornication; and perhaps the defilement which these give to the soul, that is here so clearly asserted, was not only included in the seventh commandment, but was signified and intended in many of those ceremonial pollutions under the law, for which they were to <hi type="italic">wash their clothes, and bathe their flesh in water. Whosoever looketh on a woman</hi> (not only another man's wife, as some would have it, but any woman), <hi type="italic">to lust after her, has committed adultery with her in his heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.5.28">v. 28</reference>. This command forbids not only the acts of fornication and adultery, but, (1.) All appetites to them, all lusting after the forbidden object; this is the beginning of the sin, <hi type="italic">lust conceiving</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.15">James i. 15</reference>); it is a bad step towards the sin; and where the lust is dwelt upon and approved, and the wanton desire is rolled under the tongue as a sweet morsel, it is the commission of sin, as far as the heart can do it; there wants nothing but convenient opportunity for the sin itself. <hi type="italic">Adultera mens est—The mind is debauched.</hi> Ovid. Lust is conscience baffled or biassed: biassed, if it say nothing against the sin; baffled, if it prevail not in what is says. (2.) All approaches toward them; feeding the eye with the sight of the forbidden fruit; not only looking for that end, that I may lust; but looking till I do lust, or looking to gratify the lust, where further satisfaction cannot be obtained. The eye is both the inlet and outlet of a great deal of wickedness of this kind, witness Joseph's mistress (<reference osisRef="Gen.39.7">Gen. xxxix. 7</reference>), Samson (<reference osisRef="Judg.16.1">Judg. xvi. 1</reference>), David, <reference osisRef="2Sam.11.2">2 Sam. xi. 2</reference>. We read the <hi type="italic">eyes full of adultery, that cannot cease from sin,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.14">2 Pet. ii. 14</reference>. What need have we, therefore, with holy Job, to <hi type="italic">make a covenant with our eyes,</hi> to make this bargain with them that they should have the pleasure of beholding the light of the sun and the works of God, provided they would never fasten or dwell upon any thing that might occasion impure imaginations or desires; and under this penalty, that if they did, they must smart for it in penitential tears! <reference osisRef="Job.31.1">Job xxxi. 1</reference>. What have we the covering of the eyes for, but to restrain corrupt glances, and to keep out of their defiling impressions? This forbids also the using of any other of our senses to stir up lust. If ensnaring looks are forbidden fruit, much more unclean discourses, and wanton dalliances, the fuel and bellows of this hellish fire. These precepts are hedges about the law of heart-purity, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.8">v. 8</reference>. And if looking be lust, they who dress and deck, and expose themselves, with design to be looked at and lusted after (like Jezebel, that <hi type="italic">painted her face and tired her head, and looked out at the window</hi>) are no less guilty. Men sin, but devils tempt to sin. <div eID="gen21512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21513" type="x-p"/> 2. That such looks and such dalliances are so very dangerous and destructive to the soul, that it is better to lose the eye and the hand that thus offend then to give way to the sin, and perish eternally in it. This lesson is here taught us, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.29-Matt.5.30">v. 29, 30</reference>. Corrupt nature would soon object against the prohibition of heart-adultery, that it is impossible to governed by it; "<hi type="italic">It is a hard saying, who can bear it?</hi> Flesh and blood cannot but look with pleasure upon a beautiful woman; and it is impossible to forbear lusting after and dallying with such an object." Such pretences as these will scarcely be overcome by reason, and therefore must be argued against with <hi type="italic">the terrors of the Lord,</hi> and so they are here argued against. <div eID="gen21513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21514" type="x-p"/> (1.) It is a severe operation that is here prescribed for the preventing of these fleshly lusts. <hi type="italic">If thy right eye offend thee,</hi> or <hi type="italic">cause thee to offend,</hi> by wanton glances, or wanton gazings, upon forbidden objects; <hi type="italic">if thy right hand off end thee,</hi> or <hi type="italic">cause thee to offend,</hi> by wanton dalliances; and if it were indeed impossible, as is pretended, to govern the eye and the hand, and they have been so accustomed to these wicked practices, that they will not be withheld from them; if there be no other way to restrain them (which, blessed be God, through his grace, there is), it were better for us to <hi type="italic">pluck out the eye,</hi> and <hi type="italic">cut off the hand,</hi> though the <hi type="italic">right eye,</hi> and <hi type="italic">right hand,</hi> the more honourable and useful, than to indulge them in sin to the ruin of the soul. And if this must be submitted to, at the thought of which nature startles, much more must we resolve to <hi type="italic">keep under the body, and to bring it into subjection;</hi> to live a life of mortification and self-denial; to keep a constant watch over our own hearts, and to suppress the first rising of lust and corruption there; to avoid the occasions of sin, to resist the beginnings of it, and to decline the company of those who will be a snare to us, though ever so pleasing; to keep out of harm's way, and abridge ourselves in the use of lawful things, when we find them temptations to us; and to seek unto God for his grace, and depend upon that grace daily, and so to <hi type="italic">walk in the Spirit,</hi> as that we may not <hi type="italic">fulfil the lusts of the flesh;</hi> and this will be as effectual as <hi type="italic">cutting off a right hand</hi> or <hi type="italic">pulling out a right eye;</hi> and perhaps as much against the grain to flesh and blood; it is the destruction of the old man. <div eID="gen21514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21515" type="x-p"/> (2.) It is a startling argument that is made use of to enforce this prescription (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.29">v. 29</reference>), and it is repeated in the same words (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.30">v. 30</reference>), because we are loth to hear such rough things; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.10">Isa. xxx. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">It is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish,</hi> though it be an eye or a hand, which can be worse spared, <hi type="italic">and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell.</hi> Note, [1.] It is not unbecoming a minister of the gospel to preach of hell and damnation; nay, he <hi type="italic">must</hi> do it, for Christ himself did it; and we are unfaithful to our trust, if we give not warning of <hi type="italic">the wrath to come.</hi> [2.] There are some sins from which we need to be <hi type="italic">saved with fear,</hi> particularly <hi type="italic">fleshly lusts,</hi> which are such <hi type="italic">natural brute beasts</hi> as cannot be checked, but by being frightened; cannot be kept from a forbidden tree, but by <hi type="italic">cherubim, with a flaming sword.</hi> [3.] When we are tempted to think it hard to <hi type="italic">deny ourselves,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">crucify fleshly lusts,</hi> we ought to consider how much harder it will be to lie for ever in <hi type="italic">the lake that burns with fire and brimstone;</hi> those do not know or do not believe what hell is, that will rather venture their eternal ruin in those flames, than deny themselves the gratification of a base and brutish lust. [4.] In hell there will be torments for the body; the <hi type="italic">whole body</hi> will <hi type="italic">be cast into hell,</hi> and there will be torment in every part of it; so that if we have a care of our own bodies, we shall <hi type="italic">possess them in sanctification and honour,</hi> and <hi type="italic">not in the lusts of uncleanness.</hi> [5.] Even those duties that are most unpleasant to flesh and blood, are <hi type="italic">profitable for us;</hi> and our Master requires nothing from us but what he knows to be for our advantage. <div eID="gen21515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21516" type="x-p"/> 3. That men's divorcing of their wives upon dislike, or for any other cause except adultery, however tolerated and practised among the Jews, was a violation of the seventh commandment, as it opened a door to adultery, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.31-Matt.5.32">v. 31, 32</reference>. Here observe, <div eID="gen21516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21517" type="x-p"/> (1.) How the matter now stood with reference to divorce. <hi type="italic">It hath been said</hi> (he does not say as before, <hi type="italic">It hath been said by them of old time,</hi> because this was not a precept, as those were, though the Pharisees were willing so to understand it, <reference osisRef="Matt.19.7">ch. xix. 7</reference>, but only a permission), "<hi type="italic">Whosoever shall put away his wife, let him give her a bill of divorce;</hi> let him not think to do it by word of mouth, when he is in a passion; but let him do it deliberately, by a legal instrument in writing, attested by witnesses; if he will dissolve the matrimonial bond, let him do it solemnly." Thus the law had prevented rash and hasty divorces; and perhaps at first, when writing was not so common among the Jews, that made divorces rare things; but in process of time it became very common, and this direction of how to do it, when there was just cause for it, was construed into a permission of it for any cause, <reference osisRef="Matt.19.3">ch. xix. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen21517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21518" type="x-p"/> (2.) How this matter was rectified and amended by our Saviour. He reduced the ordinance of marriage to its primitive institution: <hi type="italic">They two shall be one flesh,</hi> not to be easily separated, and therefore divorce is not to be allowed, except in case of adultery, which breaks the marriage covenant; but he that puts away his wife upon any other pretence, <hi type="italic">causeth her to commit adultery,</hi> and him also that shall marry her when she is thus divorced. Note, Those who lead others into temptation to sin, or leave them in it, or expose them to it, make themselves guilty of their sin, and will be accountable for it. This is one way of being <hi type="italic">partaker with adulterers</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.50.18">Ps. l. 18</reference>.
entries.b53a46706226baa34feac58fec009d7d8882b9a2: <div eID="gen21518" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sermon on the Mount.</title> <div sID="gen21519" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">33</hi> Again, ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time, Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths: <hi type="super">34</hi> But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God's throne: <hi type="super">35</hi> Nor by the earth; for it is his footstool: neither by Jerusalem; for it is the city of the great King. <hi type="super">36</hi> Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black. <hi type="super">37</hi> But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil. <div eID="gen21519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21520" type="x-p"/> We have here an exposition of the third commandment, which we are the more concerned right to understand, because it is particularly said, that <hi type="italic">God will not hold him guiltless,</hi> however he may hold himself, who breaks this commandment, by <hi type="italic">taking the name of the Lord in vain.</hi> Now as to this command, <div eID="gen21520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21521" type="x-p"/> I. It is agreed on all hands that it forbids perjury, forswearing, and the violation of oaths and vows, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.33">v. 33</reference>. This was said to them of old time, and is the true intent and meaning of the third commandment. <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not</hi> use, or <hi type="italic">take up, the name of God</hi> (as we do by an oath) <hi type="italic">in vain,</hi> or <hi type="italic">unto vanity,</hi> or <hi type="italic">a lie.</hi> He <hi type="italic">hath not lift up his soul unto vanity,</hi> is expounded in the next words, <hi type="italic">nor sworn deceitfully,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.24.4">Ps. xxiv. 4</reference>. Perjury is a sin condemned by the light of nature, as a complication of impiety toward God and injustice toward man, and as rendering a man highly obnoxious to the divine wrath, which was always judged to follow so infallibly upon that sin, that the forms of swearing were commonly turned into execrations or imprecations; as that, <hi type="italic">God do so to me, and more also;</hi> and with us, <hi type="italic">So help me God;</hi> wishing I may never have any help from God, if I swear falsely. Thus, by the consent of nations, have men cursed themselves, not doubting but that God would curse them, if they lied against the truth then, when they solemnly called God to witness to it. <div eID="gen21521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21522" type="x-p"/> It is added, from some other scriptures, <hi type="italic">but shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.30.2">Num. xxx. 2</reference>); which may be meant, either, 1. Of those promises to which God is a party, vows made to God; these must be punctually paid (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.4-Eccl.5.5">Eccl. v. 4, 5</reference>): or, 2. Of those promises made to our brethren, to which God was a Witness, he being appealed to concerning our sincerity; these must be <hi type="italic">performed to the Lord,</hi> with an eye to him, and for his sake: for to him, by ratifying the promises with an oath, we have made ourselves debtors; and if we break a promise so ratified, <hi type="italic">we have not lied unto men</hi> only, <hi type="italic">but unto God.</hi> <div eID="gen21522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21523" type="x-p"/> II. It is here added, that the commandment does not only forbid false swearing, but all rash, unnecessary swearing: <hi type="italic">Swear not at all,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.5.34">v. 34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.12">Compare Jam. v. 12</reference>. Not that all swearing is sinful; so far from that, if rightly done, it is a part of religious worship, and we in it <hi type="italic">give unto God the glory due to his name.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Deut.6.13">Deut. vi. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.10.20">x. 20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.23">Isa. xlv. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.4.2">Jer. iv. 2</reference>. We find Paul confirming what he said by such solemnities (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.23">2 Cor. i. 23</reference>), when there was a necessity for it. In swearing, we pawn the truth of something known, to confirm the truth of something doubtful or unknown; we appeal to a greater knowledge, to a higher court, and imprecate the vengeance of a righteous Judge, if we swear deceitfully. <div eID="gen21523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21524" type="x-p"/> Now the mind of Christ in this matter is, <div eID="gen21524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21525" type="x-p"/> 1. That we must <hi type="italic">not swear at all,</hi> but when we are duly called to it, and justice or charity to our brother, or respect to the commonwealth, make it necessary for <hi type="italic">the end of strife</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.6.16">Heb. vi. 16</reference>), of which necessity the civil magistrate is ordinarily to be the judge. We may be sworn, but we must now swear; we may be adjured, and so obliged to it, but we must not thrust ourselves upon it for our own worldly advantage. <div eID="gen21525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21526" type="x-p"/> 2. That we must not swear lightly and irreverently, in common discourse: it is a very great sin to make a ludicrous appeal to the glorious Majesty of heaven, which, being a sacred thing, ought always to be very serious: it is a gross profanation of God's holy name, and of one of the holy things which the <hi type="italic">children of Israel sanctify to the Lord:</hi> it is a sin that has no cloak, no excuse for it, and therefore a sign of a graceless heart, in which enmity to God reigns: <hi type="italic">Thine enemies take thy name in vain.</hi> <div eID="gen21526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21527" type="x-p"/> 3. That we must in a special manner avoid promissory oaths, of which Christ more particularly speaks here, for they are oaths that are to be performed. The influence of an affirmative oath immediately ceases, when we have faithfully discovered the truth, and the whole truth; but a promissory oath binds so long, and may be so many ways broken, by the surprise as well as strength of a temptation, that it is not to be used but upon great necessity: the frequent requiring and using of oaths, is a reflection upon Christians, who should be of such acknowledged fidelity, as that their sober words should be as sacred as their solemn oaths. <div eID="gen21527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21528" type="x-p"/> 4. That we must not swear by any other creature. It should seem there were some, who, in civility (as they thought) to the name of God, would not make use of that in swearing, but would swear <hi type="italic">by heaven or earth, &c.</hi> This Christ forbids here (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.34">v. 34</reference>) and shows that there is nothing we can swear by, but it is some way or other related to God, who is the Fountain of all beings, and therefore that it is as dangerous to swear by them, as it is to swear by God himself: it is the verity of the creature that is laid at stake; now that cannot be an instrument of testimony, but as it has regard to God, who is the <hi type="italic">summum verum—the chief Truth.</hi> As for instance, <div eID="gen21528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21529" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">Swear not by the heaven;</hi> "As sure as there is a heaven, this is true;" <hi type="italic">for it is God's throne,</hi> where he resides, and in a particular manner manifests his glory, as a Prince upon his throne: this being the inseparable dignity of the upper world, you cannot <hi type="italic">swear by heaven,</hi> but you swear by God himself. <div eID="gen21529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21530" type="x-p"/> (2.) <hi type="italic">Nor by the earth, for it is his footstool.</hi> He governs the motions of this lower world; as he rules in heaven, so he rules over the earth; and though under his feet, yet it is also under his eye and care, and stands in relation to him as his, <reference osisRef="Ps.24.1">Ps. xxiv. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">The earth is the Lord's;</hi> so that in swearing by it, you swear by its Owner. <div eID="gen21530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21531" type="x-p"/> (3.) <hi type="italic">Neither by Jerusalem,</hi> a place for which the Jews had such a veneration, that they could not speak of any thing more sacred to <hi type="italic">swear by;</hi> but beside the common reference Jerusalem has to God, as part of the earth, it is in special relation to him, <hi type="italic">for it is the city of the great King</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.48.2">Ps. xlviii. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">the city of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.46.4">Ps. xlvi. 4</reference>), he is therefore interested in it, and in every oath taken by it. <div eID="gen21531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21532" type="x-p"/> (4.) "<hi type="italic">Neither shalt thou swear by the head;</hi> though it be near thee, and an essential part of thee, yet it is more God's than thine; for he made it, and formed all the springs and powers of it; whereas thou thyself canst not, from any natural intrinsic influence, change the colour of <hi type="italic">one hair,</hi> so as to make <hi type="italic">it white or black;</hi> so that thou canst not <hi type="italic">swear by thy head,</hi> but thou swearest by him who is the <hi type="italic">Life of thy head,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the Lifter up of it.</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.3.3">Ps. iii. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen21532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21533" type="x-p"/> 5. That therefore in all our communications we must content ourselves with, <hi type="italic">Yea, yea,</hi> and <hi type="italic">nay, nay,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.5.37">v. 37</reference>. In ordinary discourse, if we affirm a thing, let us only say, <hi type="italic">Yea,</hi> it is so; and, if need be, to evidence our assurance of a thing, we may double it, and say, <hi type="italic">Yea, yea,</hi> indeed it is so: <hi type="italic">Verily, verily,</hi> was our Saviour's <hi type="italic">yea, yea.</hi> So if we deny a thing, let is suffice to say, No; or if it be requisite, to repeat the denial, and say, No, no; and if our fidelity be known, that will suffice to gain us credit; and if it be questioned, to back what we say with swearing and cursing, is but to render it more suspicious. They who can <hi type="italic">swallow</hi> a profane oath, will not <hi type="italic">strain at a</hi> lie. It is a pity that this, which Christ puts in the mouths of all his disciples, should be fastened, as a name of reproach, upon a sect faulty enough other ways, when (as Dr. Hammond says) we are not forbidden any more than <hi type="italic">yea</hi> and <hi type="italic">nay,</hi> but are in a manner directed to the use of that. <div eID="gen21533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21534" type="x-p"/> The reason is observable; <hi type="italic">For whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil,</hi> though it do not amount to the iniquity of an oath. It comes <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ek tou Diabolou</hi></hi>; so an ancient copy has it: it comes <hi type="italic">from the Devil,</hi> the evil one; it comes from the corruption of men's nature, from passion and vehemence; from a reigning vanity in the mind, and a contempt of sacred things: it comes from that deceitfulness which is in men, <hi type="italic">All men are liars;</hi> therefore men use these protestations, because they are distrustful one of another, and think they cannot be believed without them. Note, Christians should, for the credit of their religion, avoid not only that which is in itself evil, but <hi type="italic">that which cometh of evil,</hi> and has <hi type="italic">the appearance of</hi> it. That may be suspected as a bad thing, which comes from a bad cause. An oath is physic, which supposes a disease.
entries.e2e7f29673e91166914260800e2813d29c731ea0: <div eID="gen21534" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sermon on the Mount.</title> <div sID="gen21535" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">38</hi> Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth: <hi type="super">39</hi> But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also. <hi type="super">40</hi> And if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have <hi type="italic">thy</hi> cloak also. <hi type="super">41</hi> And whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain. <hi type="super">42</hi> Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away. <div eID="gen21535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21536" type="x-p"/> In these verses the law of retaliation is expounded, and in a manner repealed. Observe, <div eID="gen21536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21537" type="x-p"/> I. What the <hi type="italic">Old-Testament permission</hi> was, in case of injury; and here the expression is only, <hi type="italic">Ye have heard that is has been said;</hi> not, as before, concerning the commands of the decalogue, <hi type="italic">that it has been said by,</hi> or to, <hi type="italic">them of old time.</hi> It not was a command, that every one should of necessity require such satisfaction; but they might lawfully insist upon it, if they pleased; <hi type="italic">an eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth.</hi> This we find, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.24">Exod. xxi. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.24.20">Lev. xxiv. 20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.19.21">Deut. xix. 21</reference>; in all which places it is appointed to be done by the magistrate, who <hi type="italic">bears not the sword in vain,</hi> but is <hi type="italic">the minister of God, an avenger to execute wrath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.13.4">Rom. xiii. 4</reference>. It was a direction to the judges of the Jewish nation what punishment to inflict in case of maims, for terror to such as would do mischief on the one hand, and for a restraint to such as have mischief done to them on the other hand, that they may not insist on a greater punishment than is proper: it is not <hi type="italic">a life for an eye,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">a limb for a tooth,</hi> but observe a proportion; and it is intimated (<reference osisRef="Num.35.31">Num. xxxv. 31</reference>), that the forfeiture in this case might be redeemed with money; for when it is provided that <hi type="italic">no ransom shall be taken for the life of a murderer,</hi> it is supposed that for maims a pecuniary satisfaction was allowed. <div eID="gen21537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21538" type="x-p"/> But some of the Jewish teachers, who were not the most compassionate men in the world, insisted upon it as necessary that such revenge should be taken, even by private persons themselves, and that there was no room left for remission, or the acceptance of satisfaction. Even now, when they were under the government of the Roman magistrates, and consequently the judicial law fell to the ground of course, yet they were still zealous for any thing that looked harsh and severe. <div eID="gen21538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21539" type="x-p"/> Now, so far this is in force with us, as a direction to magistrates, to use the sword of justice according to the good and wholesome laws of the land, for the terror of evil-doers, and the vindication of the oppressed. That judge <hi type="italic">neither feared God nor regarded man,</hi> who would not <hi type="italic">avenge</hi> the poor widow <hi type="italic">of her adversary,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.18.2-Luke.18.3">Luke xviii. 2, 3</reference>. And it is in force as a rule to lawgivers, to provide accordingly, and wisely to apportion punishments to crimes, for the restraint of rapine and violence, and the protection of innocency. <div eID="gen21539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21540" type="x-p"/> II. What the <hi type="italic">New-Testament precept</hi> is, as to the complainant himself, his duty is, to <hi type="italic">forgive the injury</hi> as done to himself, and no further to insist upon the punishment of it than is necessary to the public good: and this precept is consonant to the meekness of Christ, and the gentleness of his yoke. <div eID="gen21540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21541" type="x-p"/> Two things Christ teaches us here: <div eID="gen21541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21542" type="x-p"/> 1. We must not be revengeful (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.39">v. 39</reference>); <hi type="italic">I say unto you, that ye resist not evil;</hi>—the evil person that is injurious to you. The resisting of any ill attempt upon us, is here as generally and expressly forbidden, as <hi type="italic">the resisting of the higher powers</hi> is (<reference osisRef="Rom.13.2">Rom. xiii. 2</reference>); and yet this does not repeal the law of self-preservation, and the care we are to take of our families; we may <hi type="italic">avoid evil,</hi> and may <hi type="italic">resist</hi> it, so far as is necessary to our own security; but we must not <hi type="italic">render evil for evil,</hi> must not bear a grudge, nor avenge ourselves, nor study to be even with those that have treated us unkindly, but we must go beyond them by forgiving them, <reference osisRef="Prov.20.22">Prov. xx. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.29">xxiv. 29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.25.21-Prov.25.22">xxv. 21, 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.12.7">Rom. xii. 7</reference>. The law of retaliation must be made consistent with the law of love: nor, if any have injured us, is our recompence in our own hands, but in the hands of God, to whose wrath we must give place; and sometimes in the hands of his viceregents, where it is necessary for the preservation of the public peace; but it will not justify us in hurting our brother to say that he began, for it is the second blow that makes the quarrel; and when we were injured, we had an opportunity not to justify our injuring him, but to show ourselves the true disciples of Christ, by forgiving him. <div eID="gen21542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21543" type="x-p"/> Three things our Saviour specifies, to show that Christians must patiently yield to those who bear hard upon them, rather than contend; and these include others. <div eID="gen21543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21544" type="x-p"/> (1.) A blow on the cheek, which is an injury to me in my body; "<hi type="italic">Whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek,</hi>" which is not only a hurt, but an affront and indignity (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.20">2 Cor. xi. 20</reference>), if a man in anger or scorn thus abuse thee, "<hi type="italic">turn to him the other cheek;</hi>" that is, "instead of avenging that injury, prepare for another, and bear it patiently: give not the rude man as good as he brings; do not challenge him, nor enter an action against him; if it be necessary to the public peace that he be bound to his good behaviour, leave that to the magistrate; but for thine own part, it will ordinarily be the wisest course to pass it by, and take no further notice of it: there are no bones broken, no great harm done, forgive it and forget it; and if proud fools think the worse of thee, and laugh at thee for it, all wise men will value and honour thee for it, as a follower of the blessed Jesus, who, though he was the Judge of Israel, did not smite those who smote him on the cheek," <reference osisRef="Mic.5.1">Micah v. 1</reference>. Though this may perhaps, with some base spirits, expose us to the like affront another time, and so it is, in effect, to <hi type="italic">turn the other cheek,</hi> yet let not that disturb us, but let us trust God and his providence to protect us in the way of our duty. Perhaps, the forgiving of one injury may prevent another, when the avenging of it would but draw on another; some will be overcome by submission, who by resistance would but be the more exasperated, <reference osisRef="Prov.25.22">Prov. xxv. 22</reference>. However, our recompence is in Christ's hands, who will reward us with eternal glory for the shame we thus patiently endure; and though it be not directly inflicted, it if be quietly borne for conscience' sake, and in conformity to Christ's example, it shall be put upon the score of suffering for Christ. <div eID="gen21544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21545" type="x-p"/> (2.) The loss of a coat, which is a wrong to me in my estate (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.40">v. 40</reference>); <hi type="italic">If any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat.</hi> It is a hard case. Note, It is common for legal processes to be made use of for the doing of greatest injuries. Though judges be just and circumspect, yet it is possible for bad men who make no conscience of oaths and forgeries, by course of law to force off the coat from a man's back. <hi type="italic">Marvel not at the matter</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.8">Eccl. v. 8</reference>), but, in such a case, rather than go to the law by way of revenge, rather than exhibit a cross bill, or stand out to the utmost, in defence of that which is thy undoubted right, <hi type="italic">let him</hi> even take <hi type="italic">thy cloak also.</hi> If the matter be small, which we may lose without an considerable damage to our families, it is good to submit to it for peace' sake. "It will not cost thee so much to buy another cloak, as it will cost thee by course of law to recover that; and therefore unless thou canst get it again by fair means, it is better to let him take it." <div eID="gen21545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21546" type="x-p"/> (3.) The going a mile by constraint, which is a wrong to me in my liberty (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.41">v. 41</reference>); "<hi type="italic">Whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile,</hi> to run an errand for him, or to wait upon him, grudge not at it, but <hi type="italic">go with him two miles</hi> rather than fall out with him:" say not, "I would do it, if I were not compelled to it, but I hate to be forced;" rather say, "Therefore I will do it, for otherwise there will be a quarrel;" and it is better to serve him, than to serve thy own lusts of pride and revenge. Some give this sense of it: The Jews taught that the disciples of the wise, and the students of the law, were not to be pressed, as others might, by the king's officers, to travel upon the public service; but Christ will not have his disciples to insist upon this privilege, but to comply rather than offend the government. The sum of all is, that Christians must not be litigious; small injuries must be submitted to, and no notice taken of them; and if the injury be such as requires us to seek reparation, it must be for a good end, and without thought of revenge: though we must not invite injuries, yet we must meet them cheerfully in the way of duty, and make the best of them. If any say, Flesh and blood cannot pass by such an affront, let them remember, that <hi type="italic">flesh and blood shall not inherit the kingdom of God.</hi> <div eID="gen21546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21547" type="x-p"/> 2. We must be charitable and beneficent (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.42">v. 42</reference>); must not only do no hurt to our neighbours, but labour to do them all the good we can. (1.) We must be ready to give; "<hi type="italic">Give to him that asketh thee.</hi> If thou has an ability, look upon the request of the poor as giving thee an opportunity for the duty of almsgiving." When a real object of charity presents itself, we should give at the first word: <hi type="italic">Give a portion to seven, and also to eight;</hi> yet the affairs of our charity must be <hi type="italic">guided with discretion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.112.5">Ps. cxii. 5</reference>), lest we give that to the idle and unworthy, which should be given to those that are necessitous, and deserve well. What God says to us, we should be ready to say to our poor brethren, <hi type="italic">Ask, and it shall be given you.</hi> (2.) We must be ready to lend. This is sometimes as great a piece of charity as giving; as it not only relieves the present exigency, but obliges the borrower to providence, industry, and honesty; and therefore, "<hi type="italic">From him that would borrow of thee</hi> something to live on, or something to trade on, <hi type="italic">turn not thou away:</hi> shun not those that thou knowest have such a request to make of thee, nor contrive excuses to shake them off." Be easy of access to him <hi type="italic">that would borrow:</hi> though he be bashful, and have not confidence to make known his case and beg the favour, yet thou knowest both his need and his desire, and therefore offer him the kindness. <hi type="italic">Exorabor antequam rogor; honestis precibus occuram—I will be prevailed on before I am entreated; I will anticipate the becoming petition.</hi> Seneca, <hi type="italic">De Vit&#226; Beat&#226;.</hi> It becomes us to be thus forward in acts of kindness, for before we call, God hears us, and <hi type="italic">prevents us with the blessings of his goodness.</hi>
entries.6d593bccd56f48e78078d749ff484a53970be886: <div eID="gen21547" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sermon on the Mount.</title> <div sID="gen21548" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">43</hi> Ye have heard that it hath been said, Thou shalt love thy neighbour, and hate thine enemy. <hi type="super">44</hi> But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you; <hi type="super">45</hi> That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust. <hi type="super">46</hi> For if ye love them which love you, what reward have ye? do not even the publicans the same? <hi type="super">47</hi> And if ye salute your brethren only, what do ye more <hi type="italic">than others?</hi> do not even the publicans so? <hi type="super">48</hi> Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect. <div eID="gen21548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21549" type="x-p"/> We have here, lastly, an exposition of that great fundamental law of the second table, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt love thy neighbour,</hi> which was the fulfilling of the law. <div eID="gen21549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21550" type="x-p"/> I. See here how this law was corrupted by the comments of the Jewish teachers, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.43">v. 43</reference>. God said, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt love thy neighbour;</hi> and by <hi type="italic">neighbour</hi> they understood those only of their own country, nation, and religion; and those only that they were pleased to look upon as their friends: yet this was not the worst; from this command, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt love thy neighbour,</hi> they were willing to infer what God never designed; <hi type="italic">Thou shalt hate thine enemy;</hi> and they looked upon whom they pleased as their enemies, thus making void the great command of God by their traditions, though there were express laws to the contrary, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.4-Exod.23.5">Exod. xxiii. 4, 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.23.7">Deut. xxiii. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite, nor an Egyptian,</hi> though these nations had been as much enemies to Israel as any whatsoever. It was true, God appointed them to destroy the seven devoted nations of Canaan, and not to make leagues with them; but there was a particular reason for it—to make room for Israel, and that they might not be <hi type="italic">snares to them;</hi> but it was very ill-natured from hence to infer, that they must hate all their enemies; yet the moral philosophy of the heathen then allowed this. It is Cicero's rule, <hi type="italic">Nemini nocere nisi prius lacessitum injuri&#226;—To injure no one, unless previously injured. De Offic.</hi> See how willing corrupt passions are to fetch countenance from the word of God, and to <hi type="italic">take occasion by the commandment</hi> to justify themselves. <div eID="gen21550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21551" type="x-p"/> II. See how it is cleared by the command of the Lord Jesus, who teaches us another lesson: "<hi type="italic">But I say unto you, I,</hi> who come to be the great Peace-Maker, the general Reconciler, who loved you when you were strangers and enemies, <hi type="italic">I say, Love your enemies,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Matt.5.44">v. 44</reference>. Though men are ever so bad themselves, and carry it ever so basely towards us, yet that does not discharge us from the great debt we owe them, of love to our kind, love to our kin. We cannot but find ourselves very prone to wish the hurt, or at least very coldly to desire the good, of those <hi type="italic">that hate</hi> us, and have been abusive to us; but that which is at the bottom hereof is a root of bitterness, which must be plucked up, and a remnant of corrupt nature which grace must conquer. Note, it is the great duty of Christians to <hi type="italic">love their enemies;</hi> we cannot have complacency in one that is openly wicked and profane, nor put a confidence in one that we know to be deceitful; nor are we to love all alike; but we must pay respect to the human nature, and so far <hi type="italic">honour all men:</hi> we must take notice, with pleasure, of that even in our enemies which is amiable and commendable; ingenuousness, good temper, learning, and moral virtue, kindness to others, profession of religion, &c., and love that, though they are our enemies. We must have a compassion for them, and a good will toward them. We are here told, <div eID="gen21551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21552" type="x-p"/> 1. That we must <hi type="italic">speak</hi> well of them: <hi type="italic">Bless them that curse you.</hi> When we speak to them, we must answer their revilings with courteous and friendly words, and <hi type="italic">not render railing for railing;</hi> behind their backs we must commend that in them which is commendable, and when we have said all the good we can of them, not be forward to say any thing more. See <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.9">1 Pet. iii. 9</reference>. They, in whose tongues is <hi type="italic">the law of kindness,</hi> can give good words to those who give bad words to them. <div eID="gen21552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21553" type="x-p"/> 2. That we must <hi type="italic">do</hi> well to them: "<hi type="italic">Do good to them that hate you,</hi> and that will be a better proof of love than good words. Be ready to do them all the real kindness that you can, and glad of an opportunity to do it, in their bodies, estates, names, families; and especially to do good to their souls." It was said of Archbishop Cranmer, that the way to make him a friend was to do him an ill turn; so many did he serve who had disobliged him. <div eID="gen21553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21554" type="x-p"/> 3. We must <hi type="italic">pray for them:</hi> <hi type="italic">Pray for them that despitefully use you, and persecute you.</hi> Note, (1.) It is no new thing for the most excellent saints to be hated, and cursed, and persecuted, and despitefully used, by wicked people; Christ himself was so treated. (2.) That when at any time we meet with such usage, we have an opportunity of showing our conformity both to the precept and to the example of Christ, by praying for them who thus abuse us. If we cannot otherwise testify our love to them, yet this way we may without ostentation, and it is such a way as surely we durst not dissemble in. We must pray that God will forgive them, that they may never fare the worse for any thing they have done against us, and that he would make them to be at peace with us; and this is one way of making them so. Plutarch, in his Laconic Apophthegms, has this of Aristo; when one commended Cleomenes's saying, who, being asked <hi type="italic">what a good king should do,</hi> replied, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Tous men philous euergetein, tous de echthrous kakos poiein</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Good turns to his friends, and evil to his enemies;</hi> he said, How much better is it <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">tous men philous euergetein, tous de echthrous philous poiein</hi></hi>—to <hi type="italic">do good to our friends, and make friends of our enemies.</hi> This is <hi type="italic">heaping coals of fire on their heads.</hi> <div eID="gen21554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21555" type="x-p"/> Two reasons are here given to enforce this command (which sounds so harsh) of <hi type="italic">loving our enemies.</hi> We must do it, <div eID="gen21555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21556" type="x-p"/> [1.] That we may be <hi type="italic">like God our Father;</hi> "that ye may be, may approve yourselves to be, <hi type="italic">the children of your Father which is in heaven.</hi>" Can we write a better copy? It is a copy in which love to the worst of enemies is reconciled to, and consistent with, infinite purity and holiness. God <hi type="italic">maketh his sun to rise,</hi> and <hi type="italic">sendeth rain,</hi> on <hi type="italic">the just and the unjust,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.5.45">v. 45</reference>. Note, <hi type="italic">First, Sunshine</hi> and <hi type="italic">rain</hi> are great blessings to the world, and they come from God. It is <hi type="italic">his sun</hi> that <hi type="italic">shines,</hi> and the rain is sent by him. They do not come of course, or by chance, but from God. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Common mercies must be valued as instances and proofs of the goodness of God, who in them shows himself a bountiful Benefactor to the world of mankind, who would be very miserable without these favours, and are utterly unworthy of the least of them. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> These gifts of common providence are dispensed indifferently to <hi type="italic">good</hi> and <hi type="italic">evil, just</hi> and <hi type="italic">unjust;</hi> so that we cannot know <hi type="italic">love</hi> and <hi type="italic">hatred</hi> by what is <hi type="italic">before us,</hi> but by what is <hi type="italic">within us;</hi> not by the shining of the sun on our heads, but by the rising of the Sun of Righteousness in our hearts. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> The worst of men partake of the comforts of this life in common with others, though they abuse them, and fight against God with his own weapons; which is an amazing instance of God's patience and bounty. It was but once that God forbade his sun to shine on the Egyptians, when the Israelites had <hi type="italic">light in their dwellings;</hi> God could make such a distinction every day. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> The gifts of God's bounty to wicked men that are in rebellion against him, teach us to <hi type="italic">do good to those that hate us;</hi> especially considering, that though there is in us a carnal mind which is enmity to God, yet we share in his bounty. <hi type="italic">Sixthly,</hi> Those only will be accepted as the children of God, who study to resemble him, particularly in his goodness. <div eID="gen21556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21557" type="x-p"/> [2.] That we may herein <hi type="italic">do more than others,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.5.46-Matt.5.47">v. 46, 47</reference>. <hi type="italic">First, Publicans love their friends.</hi> Nature inclines them to it; interest directs them to it. To do good to them who do good to us, is a common piece of humanity, which even those whom the Jews hated and despised could give as good proofs as of the best of them. The publicans were men of no good fame, yet they were grateful to such as had helped them to their places, and courteous to those they had a dependence upon; and shall we be no better than they? In doing this we serve ourselves and consult our own advantage; and what reward can we expect for that, unless a regard to God, and a sense of duty, carrying us further than our natural inclination and worldly interest? <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> We must therefore love our enemies, that we may exceed them. If we must go beyond scribes and Pharisees, much more beyond publicans. Note, Christianity is something more than humanity. It is a serious question, and which we should frequently put to ourselves, "<hi type="italic">What do we more than others?
